10447-october-vagabonds:
Richard Le Gallienne published this autumn travel book in 1911, following a summer camp that ends as October comes. The narrator, carrying potatoes to a shack half a mile up a hillside, finds a notice on a gate-post that tells him summer is over. He tears it down with a sigh and shows it to his friend Colin.

Chapters wander through orchards, apple land, Dutch Hollow, and the Susquehanna, with fellow wayfarers, an old lady of the walnuts, and a man at Dansville. Salad and moonshine, buttermilk, and a growl about country hotels add humor. Readers get a lyrical, rambling book of autumn walks and fading summer.
1054-a-collection-of-ballads:
Andrew Lang, a Scots scholar with a love of old song, gathers here the ballads of Britain: border raids, love and murder, ghosts, and fairy brides. Each piece comes with a short note on its source and its variants, so readers can see how a song changed as singers passed it on.

Chevy Chase, Thomas the Rhymer, and the cruel mother tales all appear, in the stark, plain speech of the folk. Lang's notes add lore without dulling the verse. The book is a fine door into the ballad world, and it still serves singers, students, and lovers of old tales.
10583-holland-the-history-of-the-netherl:
Thomas Colley Grattan wrote this history of the Netherlands, with a supplementary chapter on recent events by Julian Hawthorne. An illustration shows the Duke of Alva deposing Margaret of Parma, a sign of the book's focus on struggle for freedom. Grattan traces Holland from Roman times to modern days.

Chapters move from Roman invasion and Salian Franks, through Frank settlement, Friesland's subjection, and feudal formation, to later wars and independence. Dikes, guilds, and popular privileges mark the low country's growth. Readers get a detailed, old-style national history, rich in politics and character.
10848-natalie-or-a-gem-among-the-sea-wee:
Ferna Vale published Natalie, or A Gem Among the Sea-Weeds, in 1859, dedicating her sea-flower to her darling Hattie. The preface hopes readers may be led to take up their cross in meekness and humility, seeking the path that leads the wanderer home. The first chapter, "The Sea-Flower," recalls a childhood home on a wave-lashed shore, black rocks crowned with foam, and sea-gulls in trackless flight.

Natalie's story grows from that shore, mixing seaside romance with Christian feeling. Vale writes in a tender, pious voice for young women readers. The book offers a period tale of faith, nature, and a girl likened to a gem among weeds.
1088-rolf-in-the-woods:
Ernest Thompson Seton, a naturalist who knew the woods firsthand, tells of Rolf Kittering, a boy who runs from a cruel stepfather to live in the Adirondack wilds. There an old Indian guide, Quonab, teaches him to hunt, trap, build, and read sign, and the boy grows strong and self-reliant.

The tale mixes adventure with real woodcraft lore: how to make fire, snare game, and live through winter. Rolf's tests, from a first deer to a fight with a bully, mark his path to manhood. The book charmed young readers for years, and it still serves as a story and a field guide in one.
11073-the-illustrated-alphabet-of-birds:
An 1851 alphabet book teaches children letters through birds, each with a short verse and a picture. A is an auk of the Arctic sea, living on ice where winds blow free, B a blue bird whose songs ring through the forest in early spring.

Later letters give a bald eagle on the national flag, a fish hawk on the shore, a goose whose feathers fill beds, a humming bird among flowers, an ibis in bogs. The Baldwin Library copy preserves this simple, charming primer, where natural history and ABCs learn together, one bird at a time.
11110-a-countess-from-canada-a-story-of-:
Bessie Marchant wrote this backwoods story about Katherine Radford and her brothers Miles and Phil, living in a Canadian settlement after five days of snowfall. Katherine longs to go out, Miles, thirteen, wants schooling done so he can work, and Phil teases them both. Katherine corrects Phil's grammar with crushing dignity before returning to lessons.

Later chapters follow portages, floods, fishing, a store, bartering with Indigenous traders, and a stranger who proves a friend in need. A countess, a duke, and a wedding close the story, with illustrations by Cyrus Cuneo. Marchant writes spirited girls' adventure, mixing domestic life with wilderness work. The book charms readers who enjoy Canadian frontier tales of family and enterprise.
11214-the-garies-and-their-friends:
Frank J. Webb published this 1857 novel, The Garies and Their Friends, dedicated by permission to Lady Noel Byron. Webb, a coloured young man born and reared in Philadelphia, asks whether the race held as slaves is capable of freedom, self-government, and progress. Philadelphia, on the frontier between free and slave territory, held a large population of mixed and African race, including escaping fugitives and emancipated slaves.

Webb's representations of their wealth and education are reliable, his incidents mostly true, woven by a slight web of fiction. Scenes of mob violence describe Philadelphia when agitation of slavery provoked intense opposition to free coloured people, subdued only by prompt, undaunted resistance. Harriet Beecher Stowe, recommending the book in August 1857, calls it simple and truthfully told. The novel is an early landmark of African American fiction.
11236-old-ballads:
Illustrated by John Eyre, this songbook gathers old ballads and popular songs for singing and reading aloud, from Come. Lasses and Lads and Comin' Thro' the Rye to Annie Laurie, Robin Adair, Auld Lang Syne, and Home, Sweet Home. Sea songs, love songs, and drinking songs sit together, including Tom Bowling, Black-Eyed Susan, Bonnie Dundee, and Sally in Our Alley. The contents run to more than fifty pieces.

No editor's apparatus interrupts the songs; the book is meant for use, not study. Its selection shows which tunes ordinary households still sang when it was printed. For folk-song enthusiasts, it preserves a repertoire that later collections would annotate more fully, but rarely present so plainly.
11311-the-masters-of-the-peaks-a-story-o:
Joseph A. Altsheler's 1918 novel, The Masters of the Peaks, continues his French and Indian War series with Robert Lennox, Tayoga the young Onondaga warrior, and David Willet the hunter. Chapters move through deep woods and ridges, a brave defence, taming a spy, sleeping sentinels, and an audience before Montcalm, with French officers St. Luc, Montcalm, Vaudreuil, and Wolfe among the historical figures. The sign of the bear recurs as a trail mark.

Altsheler writes boys' adventure with attention to woodcraft, tracking, and Indian diplomacy. The novel balances invented heroes against real campaigns. For young readers, it offers a long, episodic trek across the northern forests at war.
11435-small-means-and-great-ends:
Edited by Mrs. M. H. Adams in 1851, Small Means and Great Ends is a juvenile annual whose preface thanks contributors for an ample supply of articles. apologizing that some generous labors must wait another year at the publisher's disposal. Contents include the title piece, Mary Ellen, the Dead Child to its Mother, Hope, the Young Soldier, the Stolen Children. My Grandmother's Cottage, the First Oath, the Fairy's Gift, a Lesson Taught by Nature, Florence Drew, Shechem, and the Little Candle.

The annual, an experiment begun in 1845, offered young readers moral tales and verse under a motto of truth and love. Its editor's gratitude and its contributors' range show a small publishing community. For children's literature historians, the volume samples mid-century American Sunday reading.
1161-jerry-of-the-islands:
Jack London tells of Jerry, an Irish terrier born on a Solomon Islands plantation, who is stolen, sold, and passed from master to master among traders, cannibals, and sailors. The dog's loyalty, pluck, and sense of fair play carry him through jungle, ship, and village.

London writes from Jerry's point of view, giving the dog thoughts and a moral code of his own. The tale praises courage and damns cruelty, and it draws on London's own South Seas voyage. The book pairs with its sequel, Michael, Brother of Jerry, and it charms dog lovers of all ages.
12095-more-bywords:
More Bywords gathers short stories. Its contents include The Price of Blood, The Cat of Cat Copse, De Facto and De Jure, and Sigbert's Guerdon. The Beggar's Legacy, A Review of the Nieces, Come to Her Kingdom, and Mrs. Batseyes Chops follow. The Price of Blood opens with a litany: from anger and hatred and all ill will, deliver us, Lord; from lightning and tempest, deliver us; from perpetual death, deliver us.

The stories belong to the byword tradition, in which a saying, a place name, or a local legend grows into a tale. Their medieval and antiquarian flavor, with Latin tags and village settings, suits readers who liked history told as story rather than as chronicle.
12484-the-knave-of-diamonds:
Ethel M. Dell's 1912 romance takes its chapter titles from cards and fate. The Missing Heart, The Queen's Jester, The Chariot of the Gods, The Fall, The Sting of a Scorpion, The Masquerade and Vengeance are among them. A jester figure, brothers, a head of house and a champion move through a story of love, loyalty and wrong.

Dell, author of The Way of an Eagle, works in her high romantic manner, with strong feeling, sudden reversals and moral tests. The knave of the title is a player in a game where hearts are staked and lost. Readers who like Dell's earlier romances will find the same blend here: passionate heroines, proud men and a plot that turns on honour kept or broken.
13222-northern-california-oregon-and-the:
This travel book on northern California, Oregon, and the Sandwich Islands, now Hawaii, records the Pacific coast in the age of settlement. Transcriber's notes correct old spellings, from Nuuanu Valley to Mount Rainier, and fix a claim on taro fields: a square forty feet on a side feeds one person for a year. The text keeps its period voice, with corrections noted.

Passages describe taro patches narrow as a schooner's deck, walks on dikes, rides in mountain torrents, and fish ponds of hundreds of acres with wicker gates. The author also urges a plan for Native reservations as military camps, with an acre per family and days of labor in common fields. The book is valuable travel evidence, and its proposals show the paternal views of its time.
13905-john-of-the-woods:
Abbie Farwell Brown wrote John-of-the-Woods in 1909, with illustrations by E. Boyd Smith. John, a wild boy of the woods, meets tumblers, a runaway, an ox-cart, and a hunchback. Chapters follow a silver piece, a wanderer, a rescue, and the animal kingdom. A hermit, a pupil, a beau, and a wolf-brother join the tale.

Brown blends fairy tale with nature study. Animals talk, help, and teach, while humans learn kindness. A forest ramble, a hunt, and a carrier pigeon carry the plot. The book suits children who love woods and beasts. Its gentle moral, that kindness rules the animal kingdom, runs throughout.
13946-camp-and-trail-a-story-of-the-main:
Isabel Hornibrook wrote Camp and Trail, a story of the Maine woods for young readers. Chapters cover jacking for deer, a spill-out, life in a bark hut, and a coon hunt. Black ducks, beaver works, moose-calling, and Herb's yarns follow. A moose snorting like a war-horse fronts one illustration.

Neal, cocking his rifle by a pond, pauses to brace himself against nervous excitement. Boys learn woodcraft, patience, and fair hunting through camp life. A Sunday among the pines and a journey to lonelier wilds close the tale. Hornibrook writes with knowledge of Maine camps. The book suits young lovers of outdoor adventure.
14149-the-pilots-of-pomona-a-story-of-th:
Robert Leighton's Orkney story follows a schoolboy among pilots, wrecks, and island weather. Chapters run from late school mornings and Andrew Drever's school to Sandy Ericson the pilot, a hen harrier, and a Viking amulet proved true. Captain Gordon, sister Jessie, Thora, and the wreck of the Undine shape the middle, with Gray's Inn and a rescue closing the run.

Sea danger gives the book its spine. A gale beats a farmhouse front, rain and salt spray flatten Thora's flowers, and whale jawbones tremble at the gate. At sea, mist hems a boat bound for South Ronaldsay, currents drive it toward Stroma's black rocks, and the Swelkie vortex whirls it about. Native boatmen know the currents' secrets, Leighton notes, while science offers its own account. Island life, told by a boy who lived it, feels salty and true throughout.
14655-big-people-and-little-people-of-ot:
Edward R. Shaw, dean of pedagogy at New York University, wrote this 1900 children's geography, published by the American Book Company, describing how people live in other lands. Illustrations show Chinese women and children and Hindu schoolchildren.

Chapters visit China, where boys shout lessons aloud, India, where children attend school from six in the morning, and Japan, Arabia, Korea, Lapland, Greenland, Russia, Switzerland, Holland, and Patagonia. Shaw writes simply for young readers. The book is a period piece of school geography, curious and kindly in intent, dated in language. Shaw's geography lessons aimed at American schoolchildren.
14770-life-in-a-thousand-worlds:
The Reverend W. S. Harris imagines a traveller who leaves Earth and visits city after city on other worlds, gazing first at the starry firmament and then at stranger skies. Each world has its own customs, laws and ways of life, and each visit becomes a lesson in conduct.

Harris, already known for moral fables and sermons, uses these invented journeys as parables. Pride, greed, charity and faith are tried out in alien settings, so familiar faults look fresh. The prose is earnest and plain, the wonders are meant to instruct rather than merely amaze, and the whole volume reads as popular theology dressed as early science fiction.
15111-randy-and-her-friends:
Amy Brooks's 1902 children's book returns to Randy, a country girl already known from two earlier volumes, and follows her among new friends. Chapters take her through fields, a district school, a journey, and small acts of giving, with gossip and cheer mixed in. Brooks drew the pictures herself.

The stories are gentle and episodic, built on kindness, good humor, and everyday country life rather than high adventure. Randy's warmth wins over neighbors and strangers alike. For young readers, the book offers old-fashioned charm; for older ones, it recalls a time when children's tales prized manners and heart over thrills.
15800-how-to-teach-religion-principles-a:
A manual for church school teachers by George Herbert Betts, issued by the Abingdon Press in New York and Cincinnati in 1926. Betts dedicates the book to the two million teachers who hold America's religious destiny in their keeping. The Abingdon Religious Education Texts carry the volume. Principles come first, methods follow.

The teacher himself opens the book, with types of teachers and the personal factor in religious teaching. Personality, its growth, and a scale for judging it get practical treatment. Later chapters turn to lesson plans, worship, and classroom order. The manual still helps teachers who want faith taught with skill, warmth, and honest method.
15874-old-testament-legends:
A set of legends from the less-known apocryphal books of the Old Testament, by M. R. James, Provost of King's College, Cambridge. Longmans, Green and Company issued it in 1913, with ten pictures by H. J. Ford. James, a scholar of manuscripts and ghost stories alike, retells old tales in clear prose. The book suits readers who know the Bible but not its byways.

Contents run from Adam and the death of Adam and Eve, through Abraham and Aseneth, Joseph's wife, to Job. Solomon and the demons, Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, and Ahikar close the set. Satan deceiving Eve in the river fronts the pictures. James keeps the wonder of the tales without preaching. The volume opens a hidden shelf: Bible stories the churches left out.
16046-boy-blue-and-his-friends:
A book of short stories for the youngest readers by Etta Austin Blaisdell and Mary Frances Blaisdell, authors of Child Life. Little, Brown, and Company issued it in 1906, with a picture of Boy Blue and Shep playing together in the fields. The preface promises stories about old friends, which children can easily read themselves.

Readers learn why Mary's lamb went to school, what the mouse sought when he ran up the clock, and why one little pig went to market while another got lost. Answers to a great many childish whys follow. The tales stay short, simple, and kind. The book serves first readers well: nursery friends, told in words they can master alone.
16099-austin-and-his-friends:
Frederic H. Balfour's 1906 book sets out to write a cheerful ghost story, a deliberate change from the old, terrifying kind. The advertisement argues that white sheets, clanking chains, and faces behind curtains made readers afraid to go to bed, until they wished they had read Robinson Crusoe instead. Balfour's ghost, by contrast, is friendly and pleasant, shedding happiness and sunshine over the life of the man who sees him.

Austin and his friends thus mix the supernatural with warmth, humor, and everyday life, rather than horror. The frontispiece shows Daphnis at the fountain, hinting at the book's classical, sunny temper. Readers who like gentle fantasy and Edwardian wit will find this a pleasant, unusual ghost tale.
16140-the-curious-book-of-birds:
Abbie Farwell Brown's 1903 book, illustrated by E. Boyd Smith and published by Houghton Mifflin, tells what birds have meant to people through the ages. Brown contrasts modern bird books, full of nests, eggs, and feather colors, with bird history: the lore, fables, and wonders that generations have attached to birds since the world began. Her tales come from many lands and tongues.

Contents include the disobedient woodpecker from France, Mother Magpie's kindergarten from the Isle of Wight, a Roumanian goldfinch, the Greek Halcyone, a Samoan bluebird, and an Ojibway robin. Each story explains a bird's mark, song, or habit through fable. Young readers and folklore lovers will find a delightful treasury.
16251-a-book-for-kids:
C. J. Dennis's Book for Kids, first published in 1921 and later reissued as Roundabout, offers Australian verse for young readers. It opens with a very charming gentleman, old as old could be. He stares, glares, wheezes, and sneezes while urging a boy to read, heed, and keep his books. The boy will need them on a later day, the old man says. Books should be companions, never toys, the old man insists, or boys grow gawky.

Dennis dedicates the book to all good children over four and under four-and-eighty, promising youth's rare clowning to readers who look without frowning. Contents include The Baker, The Swagman, The Ant Explorer, The Pieman, The Circus, and the famous Triantiwontigongolope. Children and their elders will enjoy its rollicking, good-humored rhyme.
16476-the-rover-boys-on-land-and-sea-the:
Arthur M. Winfield, writing as the Rover Boys' author, sends the brothers from San Francisco and Santa Barbara to a yacht, a wreck, and a castaway life on seven islands. Dan Baxter turns up to cause trouble, a mate tries to seize command, and Sam meets a shark. Storms, cave defenses, and a wild beast fight fill the later chapters.

The book is the seventh Rover Boys volume but stands alone as a complete story. Winfield writes fast, clean adventure for boys, with teamwork and pluck at every turn. Fans of island tales will find a lively Robinson Crusoe variant with a whole crew of young heroes.
17019-a-string-of-amber-beads:
Martha Everts Holden's 1893 book strings short essays like beads on a thread, each with a tart title. Pieces on manners, force, laughter, bashfulness, hats, flies, and the most dangerous woman mix wit with moral talk. The author, writing as Amber, scolds shams and praises plain sense in a voice both sharp and kind.

The essays are brief, best read a few at a time, and they show a late-1800s woman speaking her mind on men, dress, health, and home. Some views belong to their age, but the humor still lands. Readers who like short, opinionated prose will enjoy dipping into this amber string of small, bright thoughts.
17020-the-false-gods:
George Horace Lorimer, author of Letters from a Self-made Merchant to His Son, wrote this 1906 novel, issued by D. Appleton in New York. A picture shows arms crushing a man against a stone breast, hinting at the tale's idol and peril. Lorimer's title points to false gods of wealth, power, and pride that lure men from true duty.

Lorimer tells a business and moral tale in the brisk, popular style that made his merchant letters famous. His hero must choose between false gods and honest work. Readers who like early 1900s American novels of business and character will find a readable, moral story, with a strong plot and a clear lesson.
17097-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-in-:
Laura Lee Hope's 1917 woodland tale takes Bunny Brown and Sue to camp in the big woods with their kin. A lost cow, a missing train, a ragged boy named Tom, and a hermit drive the plot. Sue's pie, roast corn, and attic fun keep the camp days bright. The search for a lost girl named Sallie gives the middle chapters real worry.

As in the other Bunny books, small acts of help matter most: the children feed, hide, and speak up for Tom when he needs a friend. The tale is gentle, clear, and made for young readers. It closes with toys found, kin safe, and the woods feeling less strange than at first.
17155-about-orchids:
Frederick Boyle's 1893 chat about orchids argues that growing these fine flowers need not cost a fortune. Chapters cover his own garden, sales, cool, warm, and hot kinds, a lost orchid, an orchid farm, and hybrid breeding. Colored pictures show Vanda, Cattleya, Dendrobium, and other show plants in full bloom.

Boyle writes as a friend over the garden wall, plain and keen, with tips for modest growers. His letter to the Daily News, reprinted in the preface, states his aim: spread the joy of orchids to people of small means. Plant lovers will enjoy a Victorian grower's voice, still warm and useful for anyone tempted by orchids today.
17282-an-alphabet-of-old-friends:
Walter Crane's Alphabet of Old Friends, first published in 1874, pairs each letter with a nursery rhyme and a picture. A carrion crow and a tailor open at A, ba ba black sheep follows at B, and a hen and cock trade talk at C. Dickery dock, Elizabeth and her bird's nest, a confessing daughter, and hush-a-bye baby fill later letters.

Crane's pictures, grouped in fours, match the rhymes with charm and wit. The book suits very young readers learning letters through verse they can chant. Parents and collectors of children's books will enjoy a classic alphabet where old rhymes and fine art meet on every page.
17365-child-s-book-of-water-birds:
Leavitt and Allen of New York published this small children's book on water birds in 1855. It opens with the swan, called a very beautiful bird, generally white, though a black swan has been found in Australia. The swan, the book notes, is not often seen in America, having been brought from Asia and eastern Europe into England. That plain, fact-by-fact style sets the pattern for the whole book.

Young readers meet one water bird after another, learning looks, habits, and homes in short, simple passages. The book belongs to the mid-nineteenth-century fashion for teaching natural history to children through wonder rather than system. It still charms as a period primer, gentle in tone and fond of its feathered subjects.
17627-none-other-gods:
Robert Hugh Benson, author of The Conventionalists and The Necromancers, wrote this novel with a dedicatory letter to Jack Kirkby. Benson tells Kirkby that he owes him practically all the materials for the book, since Frank, the man written about, left the greater part of his diary to Kirkby. The novel thus presents itself as built from a friend's papers.

Readers follow Frank's story through the diary's record, in Benson's earnest, Catholic manner, with the title's commandment as its moral frame. The book suits readers of Benson's religious fiction and of the Edwardian novel of conscience. Its interest lies in character and belief rather than in outward adventure.
17770-christmas-stories-and-legends:
Phebe A. Curtiss put together this 1916 Christmas book in Indianapolis, with tales and legends for children and for reading aloud. Curtiss, author of White Gifts for the King, leads with her own legend of the white gifts, then draws on Andersen, Nora Smith, and more.

Stories include The Fir Tree, The Little Match Girl, Little Piccola, the legend of the Christmas tree, Babouscka, and the boy with the box. Each piece is short, warm, and kind, with a moral tucked in the tale. Families who like old holiday readings will find this a sweet shelf of Christmas cheer, fit for the season.
17807-uncle-wiggily-in-the-woods:
Howard R. Garis, author of Sammie and Susie Littletail and the Bedtime Series of animal stories, wrote these bedtime stories of Uncle Wiggily in the woods, with pictures by Louis Wisa. The stories are named for trees and plants: Uncle Wiggily and the willow tree, the wintergreen, the slippery elm, and the sassafras lead the set.

The pulpit-jack, the violets, the high tree, the peppermint, and the birch tree follow. Readers get gentle animal tales for bedtime, in Garis's kindly, old-fashioned style. The book suits small children and readers of the Uncle Wiggily series.
18037-the-story-of-ida-pfeiffer-and-her-:
The Story of Ida Pfeiffer and Her Travels in Many Lands was printed in London in 1879 by Thomas Nelson and Sons. Its epigraph, from Shakespeare, speaks of putting a girdle round the world, and Pfeiffer earned that motto in full.

Born in Vienna in 1797, the third child of a merchant named Reyer, Ida spurned dolls for drums, swords, and guns, and shared her brothers' bold sports. Her life, journey round the world, northward trips, and last travels fill the book. It is a stirring life of a fearless woman traveler, and a fine tale for readers who love bold journeys.
18341-come-lasses-and-lads:
Randolph Caldecott's picture book sets an old May song in pictures for children, published by Frederick Warne and Company in London. Come Lasses and Lads calls young people to leave their dads and away to the May-pole, with a minstrel standing by. Every lad has his lass, and the dance begins.

Willy has gotten his Jill, Johnny has got his Jone, and the dancers jigg it up and down. Watt calls strike up, Kate agrees, and Hodge and Madge declare it a holiday. Hats come off, girls curtsy on the grass, and Hall and Mall lead up Packington's Pound while Noll and Doll object. Children get a May Day in rhyme and picture: music, dance, and holiday cheer in Caldecott's lively style.
18488-the-place-beyond-the-winds:
Harriet T. Comstock wrote this novel, published by Doubleday, Page in Garden City, New York, in 1914, with pictures by Harry Spafford Potter. The Place Beyond the Winds opens with Priscilla Glenn standing on a slope from the farmhouse to the spring, lifting her head like a young deer sensing something new or dangerous. A May day more like June fills Kenmore, where seasons lapse into each other calmly.

Illustrations promise a dance grotesque, pagan, and yet divine, bottles whirling and crashing on rocks near a roadway, a threatened marriage bargain, and a sick man's flash of regained consciousness. Later plates speak of Dreamer's Rock and the open sea. Readers get a romance of a quiet place stirred by passion: a girl, a farm, and a world beyond the winds that calls her out.
18570-yule-tide-in-many-lands:
Mary P. Pringle, reference librarian of the Minnesota Public Library Commission, and Clara A. Urann wrote this Christmas book, published by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1916, with pictures by L. J. Bridgman and from photographs. Its epigraph from Tennyson speaks of the old order changing and God fulfilling himself in many ways.

Chapters take up the yule-tide of the ancients, then England, Germany, Scandinavia, Russia, France, Italy, Spain, and America. The book compares how each land keeps Christmas, from old customs to new ones. It serves as a gentle guide for readers who want to know how the feast is kept beyond their own homes.
1901-secrets-of-the-woods:
William J. Long's Secrets of the Woods is the third book of his Wood Folk series. It is another chapter in the shy wild life of fields and woods that he began in Ways of Wood Folk. Dedicated to Ch'geegee, the little friend whose coming makes winter glad, the book follows birds and beasts through their seasons.

Long writes of a neat animal detesting smells and filth. He writes of its savage attacks on Keeonekh when caught in a good place, with the close watching that made his books popular and controversial. Readers who like nature writing from direct sight will enjoy the book's patient detail, and its stories of wild neighbors told as if they were people.
19131-golden-lads:
Arthur Gleason and Helen Hayes Gleason wrote this 1916 book on golden lads, young soldiers of the Western Front, with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt. A photo shows French Fusiliers Marins, called demoiselles au pompon rouge for their youth and red cap tassels. The book mourns youth cut down in war.

Helen Gleason writes from Belgium on Germany's spy system, a silent, peaceful invasion of agents, gun foundations, and bought peasants before the deadly pounce. Such preparation, she argues, served a state beyond good and evil. Readers get a wartime tribute and warning, fierce in its Allied faith.
1918-long-odds:
H. Rider Haggard's Long Odds, reprinted in Allan's Wife and Other Tales, is narrated by a hunter. He tells how a story came to him, and turns for his rifle in a wagon when danger closes in. Getting his foot on the wheel and flinging himself toward the box, he faces odds that give the tale its name.

The story is short and tense, built on a single hunt and a single gamble, and it shows Haggard's gift for the African tale in miniature. Readers who know his longer novels will enjoy the compression: a hunter, a beast, and a wager, told with the same plain energy that carries King Solomon's Mines.
19195-rollo-in-the-woods:
Jacob Abbott wrote this 1857 Rollo story book about Rollo at play in the woods. Rollo, James, and Jonas build a wigwam, cross a tree bridge, and learn small lessons in conduct as hearts go wrong and right again. The book is one of Abbott's moral tales for young children.

Uncle George sends the boys half dollars, and Rollo tries to pry the eagle off his coin with a pin and stone, only to scratch the silver. Jonas smiles at the folly, and work on the wigwam resumes. Young readers get a gentle, instructive woodland tale of play, patience, and good sense.
19225-joyce-of-the-north-woods:
Harriet T. Comstock wrote this 1911 north woods novel, Joyce of the North Woods, with pictures by John Cassel, dedicated to Evelina Heminway Smith. Joyce Birkdale lives among loggers, cabins, and dogs, while Jude, a young man who meant to annex her to his cabin, dog, and gun, watches her meet another man in a meadow. The front piece promises winning cards in the playing.

Jude burns as a tall man waves his hat and a girl in a blue-checked gown, pale hair shining, meets him midway and slips from his arms to look up at him. Love, jealousy, and logging life drive the tale. Readers get a romantic north woods novel of strong wills and wild country.
19336-the-tangled-threads:
Eleanor H. Porter wrote this 1919 story collection, The Tangled Threads. Tales include A Delayed Heritage, The Folly of Wisdom, and Crumbs. Angelus, The Lady in Black, and Millionaire Mike's Thanksgiving also appear. The threads are lives crossed by kindness, loss, and small acts of grace. Porter was known for warm, moral fiction.

Hester, a poor mother, improvises on piano keys when children are at school. She frees years of longing in marches and dances. Daughter Penelope, home early, weeps to learn her mother can play so. Readers get tender, hopeful stories of home, music, and the hidden gifts of ordinary folk.
19359-the-patient-observer-and-his-frien:
Simeon Strunsky wrote this book of short humorous essays on city life, released by a New York publisher in the early nineteen teens. The patient observer of the title watches cowards, doctors, churches, and crowds, and reports what he sees with dry wit. Many pieces first ran in newspapers and magazines.

One sketch lets children plead with a mayor for the right simply to grow up, a joke with a serious edge. Strunsky's gift is to find the comic side of solemn things without malice. The book reads as a gentle satire of New York manners a century ago.
19660-man-of-many-minds:
E. Everett Evans wrote science fiction for the pulp magazines of the mid-twentieth century. Man of Many Minds is one of his space adventure novels. Its hero, Hanlon, stands before a feared commandant in the opening pages. He fights to hold the man's gaze and mostly fails. The desk between them bristles with communicator studs and plates.

Evans built his stories on fast action and strange mental powers. The title promises a hero whose mind is his main weapon. Pulp readers wanted danger, gadgets, and a tense standoff on page one. Evans delivers that in the first scene. The novel is a sample of the era's brisk, idea-driven space opera.
19882-itinerary-through-corsica-by-its-r:
An Itinerary Through Corsica maps the island by rail, carriage, and forest roads. Edward Lear traveled Corsica and kept a journal of the tour. The guide tradition behind it covers baths, passes, and the Riviera too. Corsica itself is the draw: mountains, forests, and Napoleon's birthplace. Roads there were few, so routes mattered greatly. An itinerary told travelers exactly where each day ended.

Lear, famous for nonsense verse, was also a serious landscape artist. His Corsican journal mixes routes with scenery and incident. Forest roads led him to the island's great pines. Such books served the new independent traveler. They replaced the courier with print. This one preserves Corsica before mass tourism arrived.
20283-women-s-wild-oats-essays-on-the-re:
Women's Wild Oats, from 1920, holds essays on the re-fixing of moral standards. One writer recalls an hour of anxious tension shared by all present. In that hour, each person seemed freed from self in a strange way. Losing individuality, they shared one universal impulse around them.

The colossal importance of that hour made itself felt to everyone. Essays here ask what rules should govern women after the war years. Suffrage, work, and freedom all pressed on old moral codes then. Readers get a sharp set of postwar essays on women and change.
20291-captain-mansana-mother-s-hands:
Captain Mansana and Mother's Hands are two tales first printed in Denmark. Captain Mansana first ran in a Danish Christmas annual, Hill and Dale. That annual was edited by a friend of the writer himself. The tale then ran through two editions in German translation.

Many friends urged the author to reissue it in his own tongue. Now it appears in separate form, paired with Mother's Hands. Scandinavian tales in English dress won many readers in that era. Readers get two tender northern stories in one small, warm volume. Both tales turn on love, duty, and the quiet strength of ordinary folk.
20341-grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-in:
Jessie Graham Flower wrote Grace Harlowe's Overland Riders in the Great North Woods. A bear under the table throws Grace's companions into sheer panic. Nora puts her foot in a platter of venison in the scramble. The guide explains that Henry, the bear, is a watch dog.

Hippy and the bear meet in hand-to-hand conflict in the fun. Grace Harlowe leads her friends on outdoor trips in this long series. North woods camps bring bears, guides, and tall tales in plenty. Readers get schoolgirl adventure with a comic, woodsy flavor throughout.
20547-stories-of-birds:
Lenore Elizabeth Mulets wrote Stories of Birds, published in 1903, to teach children the birds around them. The stories speak directly to young readers, often as if the child were talking with the bird itself. Field marks come woven into the talk.

I should have remembered your black head and throat, the child says to a chickadee. The sides of your head and neck are white, your breast and sides are light yellow. Your tail and wings are a much darker shade, daintily edged with white. Children learned to name birds by such close, friendly looking.
20560-letters-to-his-friends:
Letters to His Friends preserves the correspondence of Forbes Robinson, with a memoir of his life set before the letters. Robinson was born on November 13, 1867, in the vicarage of Keynsham, a Somerset village between Bristol and Bath. He was the eleventh child in a family of thirteen.

Eight of the children were sons and five were daughters. Their parents raised them in the close world of a country parsonage. Robinson grew into a Cambridge don and chaplain whose letters moved many readers. Friends published them after his early death, as a record of a bright, devoted life.
20561-little-ferns-for-fanny-s-little-fr:
Fanny Fern, one of America's best-loved newspaper writers, made Little Ferns for Fanny's Little Friends for the children who read her columns. The book gathers short stories and sketches sized for young hands. Fern speaks to her readers directly, as she did in print each week.

She tells the children she has some stories she hopes will please and divert them. She would rather have come and told them in person, she says, so she could see their bright faces. Since that could not be, she sends her little book instead. The warmth of that address fills every page.
20576-two-suffolk-friends:
Francis Hindes Groome wrote Two Suffolk Friends as a joint life of two East Anglian clergyman-scholars he admired. Groome is remembered for his work on Gypsy lore. Here he turns to quieter lives: Cambridge men who settled into Suffolk parishes and studies.

One friend passed to Caius College, Cambridge, and took his degree there. In 1833 he was ordained to the Suffolk curacy of Tannington-with-Brandish. Two years later he traveled through Germany as tutor to Rafael Mendizabal, son of the Spanish ambassador. Groome follows both friends through books, parishes, and friendships, in fond and learned detail.
2065-dick-hamilton-s-airship-or-a-young-:
Howard R. Garis sends Dick Hamilton, a young millionaire, into the air in this boys' adventure story. A falling biplane, a colonel's offer, and Dick's resolve lead to building an airship and a trial flight. Garis wrote boys' adventure series, including Dick Hamilton and Tom Swift, for young machine lovers.

Uncle Ezra, suspicious rivals, a rival airship, and a wreck in the clouds test Dick's courage from New York to the Pacific. Garis writes for young readers who loved machines, and the book captures the thrill of early flight. The airship itself, built in the story, reflects the real excitement over flight in the 1910s.
20650-left-end-edwards:
Ralph Henry Barbour's Left-End Edwards is a school football novel, one of his many stories of prep school sport. Edwards plays left end, the position of the title. The book follows his season: practice, rivals, injuries, and the big game that settles the year.

Edwards muses over a pamphlet he has been reading. He does not know, he says to himself with a chuckle. It is something about your mind and your body, though — never mind. He flutters the leaves and glances into the street for friends. Barbour's school tales taught a generation of boys the codes of fair play and team honor.
20669-the-oahu-college-at-the-sandwich-i: The Oahu College at the Sandwich Islands records the founding and charter of the college at Honolulu, in what is now Hawaii. Sandwich Islands was the name Captain Cook gave the Hawaiian chain. The document prints the act of incorporation and the corporation's rules. One article guards its future: trustees must fill any vacancy with all reasonable speed.
2067-beasts-men-and-gods:
Ferdinand Ossendowski recounts his flight through Mongolia and Siberia during the Russian Civil War, when a scientist and writer found himself living like a cave man among beasts, bandits, and lamas. Albert Shaw called him a twentieth-century Robinson Crusoe. Ossendowski fled the Russian Revolution through Mongolia, a journey few Europeans survived to tell.

The narrative moves from escape and hunger to strange encounters with holy men, princes, and the living Buddha, as Ossendowski crosses a land in chaos. Readers value the book for its vivid travel tale, even where its marvels invite doubt. His tales of lamas and hidden kingdoms mix travel fact with legend, which is why scholars debate the book.
21055-a-mating-in-the-wilds:
Ottwell Binns wrote this wilderness novel, published in New York by Alfred A. Knopf in 1920 as part of the Borzoi Western Stories line. It opens on a wide northern river, where a lean, grey-flecked young man paddles steadily toward his goal. Chapters promise a lost girl, a forest fire, and a brave rescue.

Around the paddler the story builds attacks at midnight, a wreck, mysterious shots, and strangers at a tent door. Names like Chigmok and Ainley carry much of the later action, told in separate accounts near the end. Readers get a fast tale of canoes, camps, and danger in the wilds.
21138-love-s-meinie-three-lectures-on-gr:
John Ruskin's three lectures on birds grew from a book begun at Brantwood in 1881, when June snow whitened the Lake District hills around him. He had planned four Oxford lectures holding the cream of forty volumes of bird science. In the end three lectures appeared: on the robin, the swallow, and the dabchicks.

Ruskin explains in a note that meinie is an old English word for a company of attendants. His birds form such a company around the reader. Close watching of feathers, flight, and habit mixes with Ruskin's wide-ranging prose. An appendix rounds out the third edition of 1897.
21300-cowboy-songs-and-other-frontier-ba:
John A. Lomax of the University of Texas collected these cowboy songs and frontier ballads as a Harvard Sheldon Fellow investigating American ballads. First published in 1910 and enlarged in 1916, the book is dedicated to Theodore Roosevelt, who encouraged the work while president. An introduction by Barrett Wendell makes the scholarly case.

Songs of the herd, the stampede, the trail, and the cowboy's death fill the pages, many with music. Lomax gathered them from working cowmen before the open range vanished. He argued the ballads held value for students of western history as well as literature. The collection helped start American folk song collecting as a serious field.
21600-the-flourishing-of-romance-and-the:
George Saintsbury edits and writes The Flourishing of Romance and the Rise of Allegory, on the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The book is the second volume of his Periods of European Literature. Matthew Arnold's line fronts the series: Europe is one great league for mind and spirit.

Saintsbury faced a plain problem: few scholars know all branches of old European writing equally. The volume surveys romance and allegory across many tongues in that rich age. W. P. Ker's Dark Ages precedes it, and F. J. Snell's Fourteenth Century follows. The set ran to twelve crown volumes at five shillings each.
21607-adrift-in-the-ice-fields:
Captain Charles W. Hall sets Adrift in the Ice-Fields among the sea ice of the Maritime Provinces in 1877. The preface promises the youth of America a taste of their neighbours' winter sports. Hall claims no great moral lesson, only true sport and true peril.

A party of English gentlemen shoots sea fowl on the ice in early spring. Hall studied the habits of each bird and beast, and the modes of their capture, with care. The land between the Straits of Canso and Hudson's Bay held leagues no white foot had trod. Drifting ice turns sport to survival in this brisk tale.
21735-the-floating-light-of-the-goodwin-:
Lightships, the floating lighthouses that guard England's worst shoals, stand at the center of this Ballantyne tale. In his preface, Ballantyne says the story shows the work and worth of these vessels and the men who crewed them. He spent a week aboard the Gull-stream light-vessel to learn the life firsthand. Trinity House officers gave him papers, books, and free run of their boats.

The Goodwin Sands, off the Kent coast, were feared by every sailor who passed them. Storms, wrecks, and long dull watches fill the chapters. Ballantyne turns a plain public service into sea adventure. Readers finish knowing why those anchored lights mattered, and what they cost the men who kept them burning.
21760-the-wonder-island-boys-adventures-:
Two boys and a grown man, cast away on a South Sea island with nothing but the clothes they wore, anchor Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys series. By hard work and cleverness they make clothing, tools, and weapons from what the island gives them. They harness natural forces, tame wild country, and in time win over the fierce tribes nearby.

Adventures on Strange Islands is one volume in the series, each book complete in itself. The boys prepare a vessel, weigh the claims of other islands, and study the customs of the peoples they meet. The publishers promised two thousand useful facts in the series. It is castaway adventure built to teach while it thrills.
21810-the-wonder-island-boys-treasures-o:
Treasure hunting drives this volume of Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys, a series about two boys and a man cast away in the South Seas. They landed with nothing but their clothes and built a new life by cleverness: tools, weapons, clothing, and command of the island's forces. Earlier books covered the caverns, the tribesmen, and a long capture and pursuit.

Here the boys listen to enemy signals, weigh signs of more than one tribe, and study old sacrifices. John and his friends Uraso and Muro carry the action. Each volume stands alone while the series rolls on. The books promised boys two thousand useful facts along with the adventure, and this one keeps the bargain.
21815-john-forster-by-one-of-his-friends:
John Forster, the friend and biographer of Dickens, gets his own short life here, written by one of his friends in 1903. Forster rose from a struggling newspaperman to chambers in Lincoln's Inn Fields, then to a mansion he built at Palace Gate, Kensington. His fine library room spoke of lettered ease. The writer calls him a man of letters of the old school.

Like Doctor Johnson, Forster led every talk he joined and scorned what he called humbug. He could be rough, despotic, and loud, yet soft-voiced with ladies and people of rank. Beneath it stood deep reading and a fine critical mind. This memoir keeps a strong Victorian personality on record, faults and force together.
21867-afterwards:
Two captives wait for a dawn that means death in the prologue of Afterwards, a desert romance by Kathlyn Rhodes. Dr. Anstice tells Miss Ryder they have only an hour before sunrise. She refuses false hope with a quiet that unnerves him. Nothing on earth, she says, can save them now, and in his heart he knows she is right.

Rhodes had written other desert tales, The Desert Dreamers and The Lure of the Desert among them. This novel flashes back from that hut at night to the road that brought them there. Old talk of a missed picnic and a visit to a temple hints at how long their absence went unnoticed. It is tense, romantic melodrama of the British desert school, built around one long night.
22223-english-songs-and-ballads:
T. W. H. Crosland compiled English Songs and Ballads for the World's Classics series in 1902. Crosland warns readers in his note that the book must not be regarded as a choice. It is simply a gathering, not a best-of. The contents run from old ballads to the drawing-room songs of the nineteenth century.

"Blow, blow, thou winter wind" stands near "Break, break, break" and the bonny brides of Scots song. Love, war, the sea, and parting fill the pages in the national manner. Cheap classics like this one put a small library of song into a coat pocket. The volume shows what Edwardians sang and quoted when they thought of English verse.
22287-smiles-a-rose-of-the-cumberlands:
Eliot H. Robinson published "Smiles": A Rose of the Cumberlands in 1919, and the public demanded more. The title page of later copies lists impression after impression: first in May 1919, tenth by August 1921. Smiles is a girl of the Kentucky Cumberland mountains. Robinson sends her among the feuds, schools, and mission workers of the hill country.

Her nickname is her character: a sunny nature set against mountain poverty and pride. A sequel, Smiling Pass, continued her career by popular request. Such Cumberland romances were a thriving kind, trading on the region's romance for lowland readers. Robinson's rose was among the most reprinted of them all.
22667-joan-of-arc-of-the-north-woods:
Holman Day wrote Joan of Arc of the North Woods, a 1922 novel of the Maine timber country. Day knew the woods and the lumber business from years as a Maine reporter, and his novels pit camp bosses, land men, and settlers against each other among the spruce.

The sample follows Latisan, a timber cruiser, down a tote road from Holeb Mountain after a week alone on the Walpole tract. He has been blazing trees for the choppers and marking twitch roads and yards. A short ax rides in his belt and calipers in one hand. With the other he feeds himself raisins from his pocket. That workmanlike portrait opens a tale whose title promises a heroine raised to lead in the woods war. Day delivers rough country and rough dealing in plenty.
22771-cattle-and-their-diseases-embracin:
Cattle and Their Diseases is a farmer's veterinary manual covering the history and breeds of cattle and the treatment of their ailments. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Before professional vets reached most farms, such a book was the stockman's doctor, consulted at the barn door.

The author had already published The Horse and His Diseases, and the public's warm reception of that book encouraged a matching volume on cattle. The spirit and general treatment are the same: breeds and their qualities first, then symptoms and remedies in plain order. Distempers, fevers, and the management of dairy and beef herds fill the pages. The manual shows nineteenth-century farming knowledge at its most practical, and its limits, on every page.
22882-image-of-the-gods:
Winter closes in on a strange settlement in Image of the Gods. The Dusties have built little furnaces to help fight the cold. What remains is tarring the fields, then buckling down beneath wind shields before the first winter storms strike. Survival here is plain, hard work.

The odd names hint at a world built from scratch, settlers facing an alien season with homemade tools. Science fiction of this kind lives on such practical detail, roofs, fuel, and weather treated as plot. The gods of the title hang over the labor, a question of what these people worship or have made. Readers get atmosphere first and answers later, in the classic magazine manner.
23031-wonderful-adventures-of-mrs-seacol:
Mary Seacole earns a famous tribute in the preface to Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands. She is the first, the writer says, who redeemed the name of sutler from suspicion of worthlessness and plunder. England, the writer trusts, will remember a woman who tended its sick, hunted up its wounded men to help them, and buried its famous dead.

Seacole's own narrative follows, from Jamaica to Panama to the Crimea. Denied an official post, she built her own British Hotel near the front and fed, doctored, and mothered an army. Her voice is brisk, funny, and proud. The memoir, published in 1857, remains one of the great personal documents of the Crimean War, and of Victorian travel.
2309-the-freelands:
John Galsworthy's Freelands follows a family of idealists on a country estate, where love, land, and politics collide. The Freelands care about tenant farmers and the open land, but their principles are tested by a daughter's marriage, a brother's ambition, and the claims of the soil itself. Galsworthy writes the English countryside with his usual care.

The novel belongs to Galsworthy's long study of property and class, quieter than the Forsyte books but just as thoughtful. Its characters argue about justice while living its contradictions. Readers of English social fiction will find a rewarding, reflective novel.
2310-in-the-carquinez-woods:
Bret Harte sets this novel in the woods of Carquinez, California, where a mysterious woman and a fugitive past disturb a quiet settlement. In the Carquinez Woods mixes mining camp intrigue with a romance shadowed by secrets, as Harte's characters sort truth from rumor under the great trees. The forest setting gives the story a brooding quality rare in his work.

The plot turns on identity and redemption, with Harte's usual sympathy for outcasts. The novel is longer and more serious than his sketches. It rewards readers who want Harte in a darker, more sustained mood.
23165-the-man-who-stole-a-meeting-house-:
J. T. Trowbridge sketches an unforgettable figure in The Man Who Stole a Meeting-House, dated 1878, from Coupon Bonds. Jedwort leans on a gatepost one particular morning, and the narrator never forgets the sight. The gate itself is too rickety to lean on. Jedwort is a grown man built like a hill, short-legged and stooping. His back swells under his shirt like a sack of grain, and the narrator never forgets the figure he cuts.

A man who steals a whole meeting-house needs building up, and Trowbridge builds him from the gatepost out. His Coupon Bonds tales deal in New England rogues and the neighbors who study them. The theft, a matter of debt, timber, and nerve, unfolds as village legend. Readers get regional humor of the first rank.
23295-grace-darling-heroine-of-the-farne:
Eva Hope's Grace Darling, Heroine of the Farne Islands tells the life of a famous lighthouse keeper's daughter. It opens with a question much argued in Hope's day: what is woman's work? Forefathers, she notes, settled that question more rapidly than her own age could.

In the long ago, she argues, women were less ambitious than in her time. Against that debate, Grace Darling's story stands as evidence. Readers get the tale of a young woman whose courage at sea made her a national heroine. Her story is told by a writer well aware of what that example proved.
23389-handbook-to-the-new-gold-fields:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote this handbook in eighteen fifty eight for readers heading to the new gold fields of British North America. Much of it quotes a Times correspondent at length, with letters from the colonial governor to the British government and the slow replies that crossed a continent and an ocean by sail.

Routes, costs, outfits, diggings, and colonial rules fill the pages, aimed at men weighing a long, risky trip for gold. Ballantyne himself called such books pot boilers beside his dashing tales for teens, and the prose is workmanlike rather than stirring. Yet for readers of gold rush history, the handbook gives a true, first hand sense of how news, hope, and hardship travelled in that hungry year.
23530-adventures-in-many-lands:
Egerton R. Young gathered this volume of adventures in many lands for the Brave Deeds series. It is uniform with tales of black troopers, races for life, heroines of the world, and heroes of flood and flame. The series spans Indian trails, Arctic realms, Irish rebellion, Australian stories, and captains' tales, all pitched at young readers who love daring deeds.

Young's own tales of Cree and Salteaux Indians, mission work, and northern travel anchor the book, with other writers adding deeds on land and sea. The prose stays brisk and moral, praising courage, faith, and endurance in far places. Boys and girls who love true life adventure, lightly fictionalised, will find a full shelf of heroes here, from prairies and ice to seas and sieges.
2360-the-riddle-of-the-sands:
Erskine Childers's Riddle of the Sands invented the modern spy novel when two amateur sailors, cruising the Frisian Islands, stumble on a German invasion plan. The narrator and his friend Davies map tidal flats, dodge patrols, and piece together the enemy's design from wrecks, charts, and fog. Childers, an expert sailor, makes the navigation itself thrilling.

The book's warning about German sea power stirred Britain before the First World War. Its realism, maps, and tides set it apart from wilder adventure tales. Spy fiction fans still count it a founding text.
23831-the-seed-of-the-toc-toc-birds:
Francis Flagg published The Seed of the Toc-Toc Birds in Astounding Stories in January 1932. Its hero, Talbot, works mining prospects far up in the Catalinas and returns toward the Mountain View Hotel in Oracle, Arizona, with his young Mexican assistant Manuel.

From an abandoned shaft behind the town emerges a bird Talbot has never seen: buzzard-large, with golden eyes, a flat reptilian head, and feathers glittering like blued copper edged with silver. Manuel crosses himself at the sight. A sidenote warns that Professor Reubens little suspects what his atom-tampering will set loose upon the world.
2384-the-deliverance-a-romance-of-the-vi:
Ellen Glasgow's Deliverance is a romance of the Virginia tobacco fields after the Civil War, where old families face ruin and new men rise. The novel follows Christopher Blake, a young Virginian who gives up his inheritance for love and honor, and the woman whose fate is bound to the land. Glasgow writes the tobacco country with a native's knowledge.

The book's power lies in its portrait of a South in transition, where pride and poverty collide. Glasgow's realism tempers the romance without killing it. Readers of Southern fiction will find an early work of a major novelist.
23960-after-a-few-words:
Seaton McKettrig's After a Few Words appeared in Analog in October 1962, with a teasing opening. History counts as a science; the rest is pure invention, as Americans well know. Its hero settles into a seat, puts on a helmet, and lifts the visor.

Before him rides the forward part of a Crusader column, lances upright and pennons flying. Knights Templars take the advance, followed by the mailed knights of Brittany and Anjou, King Guy of Jerusalem, and the host of Poitou. Sir Robert de Bouain rides with the Norman and English troops, beside the red-and-gold banner of Richard the Lionheart. McKettrig's tale is a Crusade relived through a machine.
2487-cross-roads:
Margaret E. Sangster's Cross Roads follows characters at the turning points of their lives, where choices about love, work, and faith set their futures. The novel weaves several lives together at a country crossroads, with Sangster's warm, moral voice guiding each toward a better path. Her stories were beloved by readers of family fiction.

The book's appeal lies in its sincerity and its hopeful view of human change. Modern readers will find its morals old-fashioned but its feeling genuine. It offers a window into popular fiction of its time.
2555-under-the-redwoods:
Bret Harte gathers stories of California life in this volume, from a stormy night at Sawyer's Ledge to Bohemian days in San Francisco. Jimmy's big brother comes home from California, the youngest Miss Piper charms a town, and a widow of the Santa Ana valley keeps her own counsel.

A mermaid off Lighthouse Point, three vagabonds of Trinidad, and a romance of the stage line add color and surprise. Harte writes with his usual mix of dialect comedy and tender feeling, and the redwoods stand over all as a symbol of a West already passing. The set shows his late style at its most relaxed.
2562-the-clouds:
Aristophanes wrote this comedy about Strepsiades, an Athenian farmer ruined by his son Phidippides and his debts. At midnight, sleepless with worry, Strepsiades drags his son to the Thinkery, the school of Socrates, hoping to learn the art of making the weaker argument win.

Socrates and his pale disciples teach clouds, logic, and new gods, while father and son argue with Just Cause and Unjust Cause. The jokes bite at sophists, debt, and fashionable learning, and the ending turns dark. Translated here by William James Hickie, the play still stings as a satire on clever talk that dodges honest bills.
2730-long-odds:
H. Rider Haggard tells this story as he heard it from his old friend Allan Quatermain, called Hunter Quatermain in South Africa. One evening at the place Quatermain had bought, the hunter told a tale of a wager against odds that seemed impossible.

Long Odds turns on a gamble, a hunt, and a debt of honor, with the African bush as its stage. Haggard writes in Quatermain's voice, dry and modest, letting the adventure speak. The story delights as a short, sharp sample of his art, where courage is measured against a long price.
2732-ballads:
William Makepeace Thackeray gathers his ballads in this volume, from the Chronicle of the Drum to Abd el Kader at Toulon, the Caged Hawk. The King of Brentford's Testament, The White Squall, and Peg of Limavaddy follow, with a May Day Ode and the Ballad of Bouillabaisse.

The Mahogany Tree, The Yankee Volunteers, and Mrs. Katherine's Lantern show Thackeray's range, from satire to sentiment. His verse is easy, witty, and musical, written for singing and reciting. The book offers a lighter Thackeray, rhyming his age with a smile. Thackeray sings history, satire, and sentiment in turn.
2819-barrack-room-ballads:
Rudyard Kipling's Barrack-Room Ballads gather his poems in the voice of the ordinary British soldier, known as Tommy, in India and on campaign. The first series of 1892 and the second of 1896 include Danny Deever, Gunga Din, Mandalay, The Young British Soldier, and the Widow at Windsor pieces. Kipling writes in barrack slang, with choruses meant to be sung.

The poems praise endurance, mock officers and recruits, and record cholera camps, route marches, and the boredom between battles. Their rhythm and direct speech made them popular far beyond army readers. They remain the best-known poems of soldier life from the late Victorian empire, admired and argued over in equal measure.
2831-a-bundle-of-ballads:
Henry Morley edited this anthology of old English and Scottish ballads for general readers, gathering songs that had passed from singer to singer before they reached print. Chevy Chase, the Nut-Brown Maid, Adam Bell, Barbara Allen, Sir Patrick Spens, and Robin Hood pieces sit side by side with laments, ghost songs, and comic tales. The contents list alone reads like a map of folk storytelling.

Each ballad tells its story fast, through dialogue and repeated refrains rather than description. Lovers part, outlaws escape, kings meet commoners in disguise, and the dead return to speak. Morley's selection gives a newcomer the core of the ballad tradition in one volume, with the old spellings and rhythms left close to the sources.
3013-the-birds:
Aristophanes wrote The Birds as a comic extravaganza, unlike his other surviving comedies in subject and conception. The introduction calls it a graceful, whimsical theme chosen for the opportunities it affords, and the footnotes explain Greek names, terms, ceremonies, and puns that would otherwise be lost. Two Athenians, Pisthetaerus and Euelpides, leave the city to found a city in the sky. The birds become gods, promising farmers that locusts will not eat their vine blossoms.

Owls and kestrels will devour the pests, and gnats and gall bugs will be kept in check. Pisthetaerus bargains with gods and men alike. The comedy still delights with its fantasy, wordplay, and the sheer daring of building Cloudcuckooland between earth and heaven.
3054-volcanic-islands:
Charles Darwin wrote Geological Observations on the Volcanic Islands from his Beagle voyage, covering St. Jago in the Cape Verde Islands, Fernando Noronha, Terceira, Tahiti, Ascension, St. Helena, and the Galapagos. Later chapters treat trachyte and basalt, the distribution of volcanic isles, Australia, New Zealand, and the Cape of Good Hope. An editorial note calls the observations original and admirably adapted to general readers in many parts.

Darwin describes siliceous sinter and jasper in detail, noting white, pearly, light varieties passing into pinkish quartz, and yellowish white kinds with earthy powder in small cavities. Both occur in masses in altered trachyte or in veins. The book remains a foundational work of volcanic geology, written before Darwin's evolutionary fame.
3206-moby-multiple-language-lists-of-com:
This file holds the Moby language lists, a set of public domain word lists of common words in many languages. The documentation notes trace them to the Ward word lists, among the largest free lists in the world when they joined the Gutenberg collection in 2007. They carry no accented characters or Unicode, as a newer file would. Instead they use phonetic spelling, so plain ASCII can hold them.

Such lists serve spell checkers, language learners, and software that must guess a text's tongue from its commonest words. Readers opening the file will find data, not essays: word after word, language after language, in a form built for lookup. The set remains a useful record of how free language data was shared before Unicode became the norm.
3280-cap-n-warren-s-wards:
Joseph C Lincoln, author of The Depot Master and The Woman Haters, writes this Cape Cod novel of guardianship. Cap'n Warren's wards give the book its title and its problem: a seaman turned guardian, with young charges to raise and a village watching every choice. Edmund Frederick supplied the illustrations for the 1911 Appleton edition.

An early illustration shows Captain Warren risen from his chair and facing a woman, mid-argument, on page forty-eight. That scene sets the book's tone: plain talk, stubborn kindness, and comedy from duty. Lincoln writes his coast with affection, and the wards' fortunes, like the captain's, are settled by character rather than by luck.
338-old-indian-legends:
Zitkala-Sa, a Yankton Sioux writer, retells Dakota legends for children and adults. Old Indian Legends opens with Iktomi the spider fairy, in brown deerskin leggings and beaded moccasins. His painted face and red-banded braids mark him as a trickster.

Iktomi meets ducks, muskrats, coyotes, and fawns, and always learns too late. The badger and the bear, the tree-bound red eagle, and Iya the camp-eater follow. Zitkala-Sa's English keeps the tales' humor and warning. The collection preserves Dakota storytelling in print. Zitkala-Sa later fought for Native rights in Washington.
3710-an-unprotected-female-at-the-pyrami:
Anthony Trollope turns a Nile tour into comedy in this short tale of an Englishwoman who travels Egypt without a male escort. Miss Dawkins, brisk and sure of herself, joins a party bound for the Pyramids, and her fellow travelers spend as much time judging her freedom as they do gazing at tombs. The narrator watches the clash with amused detachment, noting how a woman alone draws comment at every halt.

Donkey boys, racing lads, picnic hampers, and the long climb up the stone sides fill the day with bustle. Miss Dawkins proves more taken with Mount Sinai, which is nowhere in sight, than with the Pyramids before her nose. The tale is a light study of manners abroad, where pride, gossip, and good humor mix under a hot sun.
3791-the-reign-of-law-a-tale-of-the-kent:
James Lane Allen sets this Kentucky novel in the hemp fields where Anglo Saxon farmers first won a foothold in the western wilderness. The story opens in 1782, with hemp growing tall beside the walls of Bryan's Station while backwoods riflemen Tomlinson and Bell ride to rouse the settlements and save the west. From that frontier summer Allen follows farm folk through seasons of labor, faith, and change.

A later scene shows a workman in the dead fields at a winter sunset, dust on his throat and eyes, gazing at a great light on the dark red horizon. The moment kindles a spiritual passion in him, a flame of immortal things alive in his soul. The novel suits readers who like regional fiction where land, work, and inner life grow together.
4042-mozart-the-man-and-the-artist-as-re:
A portrait of Mozart built from his own letters shows the composer as a working artist, arguing craft with his father. Writing from Vienna in November 1780, he debates the Ghost's speech in Hamlet, warning that a speech too long breaks belief on stage.

The voice, he insists, must be terrifying and real, and length itself can betray the fiction. Such letters reveal Mozart the dramatist, thinking about effect, timing, and truth in music and theater. Readers who love Mozart will enjoy meeting him in his own plain, sharp words, far from legend.
413-ballads:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers narrative poems of far seas and old wars in this 1895 volume. The Song of Rahero tells a Tahitian legend of slaying and revenge, with notes on island custom. The Feast of Famine treats Marquesan rites, while Ticonderoga follows a Highland name across the Atlantic to war.

Shorter pieces include Heather Ale, a Galloway legend of a secret brew, and Christmas at Sea, a sailor's bleak holiday. Stevenson writes in strong, rolling verse, keen on place and fate. The book shows his gift for tale-telling in meter, from Pacific isles to Scots glens.
4205-berlin-and-sans-souci-or-frederick-:
L. Muhlbach's historical romance turns to Frederick the Great and the dancer Barbarina at Sans-Souci. Resting half reclined on a small crimson divan, arms crossed over her breast, Barbarina fixes blazing eyes on the intruders and sits petrified in stubborn silence.

She has the glance of a panther prepared for death or to slay her enemy, while the king stands quiet and waiting. Muhlbach builds court, love, and power around the Prussian king's circle. Readers who enjoy royal romance will find a dramatic tale of a dancer who would not bend.
4248-the-problem-of-the-ohio-mounds:
Cyrus Thomas wrote this study to answer a much-debated question. Who built the great earthworks of Ohio? Were they the work of a lost race, or of native peoples known to history? He weighs historical evidence, burial customs, and pottery. He also weighs stone tools and the layout of the mounds.

Later chapters test the case for the Cherokees as mound builders. They cover links to the Tallegwi of tradition. They compare mound burials with Indian practices, such as burial in dwellings and the use of fire. Thomas argues from close comparison rather than legend. The book remains a clear statement that the mounds belong to Indian history.
438-underwoods:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers verse in English and Scots in this volume, first shaped in the 1880s. Book one holds songs of the road, the sea, and friends, including the famed Requiem with its wide and starry sky. Later books turn to Scots speech, doctors, and the sickroom, with a dedication praising physicians as a rule.

Stevenson stole his title from Ben Jonson and owned the theft with a jest. His lines mix cheer, grief, and a traveler's restlessness. The book shows a poet of wide range, at home in both tongues, and it keeps his most quoted short poems in one place.
4381-the-aran-islands:
John M. Synge wrote this account of the Aran Islands off the west coast of Ireland, thirty miles from Galway. He begins with simple geography: Aranmor, nine miles long; Inishmaan, round and three and a half miles across; and Inishere, slightly smaller. Kilronan, the chief village, has changed with the fishing industry.

Synge lived among islanders, listening to their stories, songs, and speech, and watching their work in boats, fields, and stone-walled plots. The book records a world of Irish language, belief, and hardship, before modern change swept it away. It is both travel writing and a source for Synge's plays, and it remains a classic of Irish literature.
454-the-breitmann-ballads:
Charles G. Leland writes comic ballads in the voice of Hans Breitmann, a German-American whose broken English and high spirits carry him through beer halls, battles, and love affairs. The dialect is the joke and the charm. Leland created Breitmann in the 1860s, and the ballads ran in magazines before book form.

Leland, a scholar of folklore as well as a humorist, lets Breitmann blunder through American life with cheerful confidence. The ballads were hugely popular in their day, and they still read as a lively piece of nineteenth-century humour. Breitmann's German-English, full of comic errors, made him a favourite of American readers.
5149-gold-of-the-gods:
Arthur B. Reeve's mystery follows Professor Craig Kennedy into a case of Peruvian treasure, beginning with a Peruvian dagger and a soldier of fortune. Chapters run through treasure hunters, a Wall Street promoter, the curse of Mansiche, arrow poison. A poisoned cigarette appears, as Kennedy uses X-ray readers, paper fibres, and shoe prints to trace the crime.

The novel mixes archaeology with modern detection, moving from museum relics to laboratory tests. Readers of Reeve's scientific detective stories will find the usual brisk plotting. Inventive gadgets drive a treasure hunt that turns deadly.
5420-rab-and-his-friends:
John Brown, a Scottish doctor and writer, gathered these sketches and stories around the figure of Rab, a faithful dog, and his master. The collection grew from a lecture Brown gave in his native village of Biggar, where he chose to tell his listeners the story of Ailie, a patient whose courage stayed with him. Warmth, humor, and simple human feeling run through the pieces.

The best-known tale follows a poor Scottish family and their dog through illness and loss, told in Brown's plain, affectionate voice. Other sketches recall doctors, villagers, and everyday kindness in nineteenth-century Scotland. Readers looking for gentle, humane storytelling will find this short book moving without ever turning sentimental.
5762-grammar-and-vocabulary-of-the-lau-l:
Walter Ivens presents a grammar and vocabulary of the Lau language of the Solomon Islands, published by the Carnegie Institution. The transcriber notes that some fine distinctions of neighboring Saa orthography were lost, while Lau spelling stands as given. Ivens sets out sounds, word forms, and sentence patterns, then supplies a vocabulary for learners and field workers.

The book serves linguists, missionaries, and historians of the Pacific, preserving a record of Lau as spoken in its time. Readers will find a scholarly reference rather than a storybook, with paradigms and word lists as its core. Its value lies in documentation: a language community's speech, captured in print for study and for descendants seeking their heritage.
6164-the-life-of-the-fields:
Richard Jefferies gathers The Life of the Fields from magazine pieces, thanking editors who allowed reprints. The Field-Play appeared in Time, Bits of Oak Bark and The Pageant of Summer in Longman's Magazine, and Meadow Thoughts and Mind under Water in The Graphic.

Clematis Lane, Nature near Brighton, Sea, Sky, and Down, and January in the Sussex Woods came from The Standard, with other essays from art, nature, and London papers. Contents promise the pageant of summer, field play, acorn gathering, and rural dynamite. Jefferies writes country life with close eyes and a poet's patience.
6329-catalogue-of-british-columbia-birds:
The Provincial Museum at Victoria publishes this catalogue of birds proven to occur in British Columbia, with a preface that admits its incompleteness frankly. The north and northeast interior remain a valuable field for work, and distribution notes for some species stay thin. Since John Fannin's 1898 list of 339 species and subspecies, the compiler adds twenty-four more, with thanks to constant observers like A. C. Brooks of Chilliwack and the Okanagan.

Entries run in systematic order, with places and seasons noted. A red backed sandpiper is common in spring and autumn migration along island and mainland coasts, taken at Chilliwack. A semipalmated sandpiper is not uncommon on the coast and common at Metlakatla. The catalogue is a working list for naturalists, plain in form and rich in local record, valuable precisely because it names its gaps and its helpers.
6408-letters-of-anton-chekhov-to-his-fam:
Constance Garnett chooses from eighteen hundred and ninety letters published by Chekhov's family those that best show his life, character, and opinions, with a memoir abridged from his brother Mihail's sketch. Letters to his wife after marriage were not yet published when she worked. The sketch opens in 1841, when a serf of a Russian nobleman bought freedom for himself and his family. The price was three thousand five hundred roubles, seven hundred a soul, with a daughter Alexandra thrown in for nothing.

That serf's grandson was Anton Chekhov, and the nobleman's son was Tchertkov, the Tolstoyan. Chekhov writes to family and friends with a doctor's eye and a storyteller's brevity, reading Bourget's Disciple in Russian and judging him gifted, intelligent, cultured, and steeped in natural science method. Garnett's volume is a life in letters, where a grandson of a serf becomes Russia's clearest witness.
6418-five-little-peppers-and-their-frien:
Margaret Sidney dedicates this book to her daughter Margaret, who embodies Polly Pepper in girlhood for her friends. A preface explains that so many interesting friends of the Five Little Peppers deserved their own stories, and this volume gives them. A five o'clock tea opens, with Phronsie sitting in the middle of the stairs, Clem Forsythe, and Miss Taylor's working bee.

Grandma Bascom, a disappointment, a garden party, and a ten dollar bill follow, with trouble for Joel, Rachel, and doings at the parsonage. Rachel laughs at a fine lady's dignity, doubles up her thin figure, and goes off in a gust of mirth. Sidney writes warm family comedy, where friends widen the Peppers' world and kindness, not wealth, settles each trouble.
6480-on-the-study-of-words:
Richard Chenevix Trench, archbishop, delivers On the Study of Words as lectures, in a twentieth edition revised by A. L. Mayhew. Coleridge's motto opens it: language is the armoury of the human mind, holding trophies of past conquests and weapons of future ones. Trench urges something beyond books: not in books only, nor connected oral discourse, but in words contemplated singly lie boundless stores of moral and historic truth, passion, and imagination.

Lectures cover poetry in words, morality in words, history in words, rise of new words, distinction of words, and the schoolmaster's use of words. A mid passage notes how idiot came to be called innocent, one who does no hurt, assuming hurt and harm are men's chief employment. Trench writes philology as moral history, where each word carries a lesson worth learning.
6489-a-book-of-golden-deeds:
Charlotte M. Yonge asks what a golden deed is, then answers with stories from Alcestis and Antigone to the Vendeans. The cup of water, how one man saved a host, the pass of Thermopylae, and the rock of the Capitol open the book. The two friends of Syracuse, the devotion of the Decii, and Regulus follow. The brethren of Judah, the chief of the Arverni, and the last fight in the Coliseum follow. Guzman el Bueno, faithful till death, the keys of Calais, and Sempach follow.
