The constant prince, the carnival of Perth, the crown of St. Stephen, George the Triller, and Sir Thomas More's daughter sit beside heroes of plague, gunpowder perils, and soldiers in snow. A mid passage shows a penitent emperor, crown, purple robe, and buskins laid aside, prostrate before Ambrose, who pronounces forgiveness in his Master's name. Yonge writes heroism for young readers, deed by deed.
6524-stray-birds:
Tagore lines up more than three hundred tiny poems, each no more than a few lines, like birds that land, sing, and fly on. Summer birds at a window, autumn leaves with no song, desert sand begging for a tune, and tears that keep smiles in bloom all pass in quick succession. The book takes its shape from that brief, bright movement.

No poem stays long enough to grow heavy, yet many leave a clear image or a sharp turn of thought behind. Love, loss, the earth, and the small wonders of a day are the chief subjects, handled with a light hand. Stray Birds suits slow reading, a page or two at a time, with room to pause between each flash.
6742-the-school-for-husbands:
Molière's School for Husbands, first played in Paris in June 1661, was the first play to use School in its title as a promise of a lesson. The notice explains that Molière wished hearers to know he meant to teach married men, not just to amuse them, and to answer those who called theatre harmful or trivial. Sheridan and others later copied the title trick.

Two brothers, one strict and one easy, raise two wards in opposite ways, and the strict man's ward teaches him a lesson in love. The verse moves briskly, with wit as its weapon. The School for Husbands is a clever, enduring comedy on how not to rule a wife.
6851-ruth-fielding-at-snow-camp-or-lost-:
Alice Emerson sends Ruth Fielding to Snow Camp, lost in the backwoods, opening with a lively time and a surprising appearance. A newspaper clipping, the strange behavior of Fred Hatfield, and a trip off for the backwoods follow, with a train ride, a runaway in earnest, and first days at Snow Camp. Long Jerry Todd, bears, frost games, and peril with a taffy pull fill the winter.

A telephone chase, a battle in snow, a besieging storm king, a snow shroud, and a double captivity test Ruth's pluck. Emerson writes with bright, clean humor for girls. Ruth Fielding at Snow Camp is a cheerful, snowy adventure of friendship and courage.
6895-the-camp-fire-girls-go-motoring-or-:
Hildegard Frey sends the Winnebago Camp Fire Girls on an automobile trip in September, told by the group's own reporter at Nyoda's urging. The girls have just come home from Onoway House when a runaway girl, met in some distress, sets their journey in motion. Sahwah jokes that only a ride in a patrol wagon was missing, and the tale keeps that high spirited tone throughout.

Much of the fun springs from small things, including the craze for tan khaki outing suits that summer. From evening stars over a window to roads, mishaps, and new friends, Frey follows a band of girls learning to fend for themselves on the open road. Campfire loyalty is their guide.
7001-history-of-the-philippine-islands:
Antonio de Morga's history of the Philippine Islands, translated by Blair and Robertson, runs from Magellan's discovery in 1521 to the start of the seventeenth century. Morga, alcalde of criminal causes in the Royal Audiencia of New Spain and counsel for the Holy Office, wrote his Sucesos in Mexico in 1609. This volume one, issued separately from the fifty five volume Philippine Islands series, adds descriptions of Japan, China, and adjacent countries.

Appendices treat the expedition of Thomas Candish, and facsimiles accompany the text. Blair and Robertson edited and annotated the translation for the Arthur H Clark Company in 1907. The book remains a first hand Spanish account of the islands, their trade, wars, and peoples, at the dawn of colonial rule.
7381-the-eustace-diamonds:
Anthony Trollope's novel turns on a necklace and a widow who will not give it up. Lizzie Greystock, married briefly to Sir Florian Eustace, claims the Eustace diamonds as her own property. The family lawyers insist they are an heirloom that must pass to the heir. Lizzie, charming and unscrupulous, fights her case in drawing rooms, in the press, and finally in court.

Around the diamonds gather suitors, a scheming clergyman, a loyal friend in Lucy Morris, and a London world eager for scandal. Trollope uses the dispute to satirize society's greed and its love of a good story, while keeping sympathy for the people caught in the machine. The novel is one of his Palliser-era masterpieces of social comedy, sharp, funny, and unsparing.
7473-lost-on-the-moon-or-in-quest-of-the:
Roy Rockwood, the house name behind many boys' adventure series, sends his heroes to the moon in this novel. The chapters tell the plan in order. First comes a wonderful story, then something about the heroes. Then come preparing for a voyage, an accident, and the work of an enemy. At last they are ready for the moon, and off at last. A field of diamonds near the Sea of Tranquility is the prize they seek.

On the moon come torches of life, the edge of a crater, a breakdown, and the dread of being lost on the moon itself. Mark is captured, Jack is puzzled, and Washington sees a ghost, in the breathless sequence boys' fiction loved. The book is a period piece of early space adventure, written when the moon still seemed a place a clever boy might actually reach.
7552-quotes-and-images-from-motley-s-his:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the Netherlands is the classic American account of the Dutch revolt against Spain, and this volume gathers its quotations and images. Illustrations show the siege of Antwerp, William of Orange, called the Silent, the Earl of Leicester, Alexander Farnese, Prince of Parma, and John of Barneveld. The Hague in 1566, the last year of peace, opens the story.

The quotations catch Motley's republican spirit: a pleasantry called voluntary contributions or benevolences, a good lawyer is a bad Christian, and a common hatred united the provinces for a time at least. In that republic, the notes add, it was a penal offence to talk of peace or truce. The collection is a doorway into Motley's great narrative of a small country disinherited by nature, winning its freedom.
7776-the-call-of-the-cumberlands:
Charles Neville Buck's The Call of the Cumberlands opens near the backbone of the Cumberland ridge, where sun hesitates above a sugar-loaf cone over Misery Creek. Light still crowns the hillsides while gloom thickens below, where water tosses in small cascades between mossy boulders.

A native would know the rough creek bed as a country road, though no traveler passes now, save a partridge calling Bob White and a cardinal flashing among pines. Through mountain speech and feud country, the novel follows families bound to these hills, and a call home that proves hard to refuse.
7801-five-little-friends:
Sherred Willcox Adams's Five Little Friends, pictured by Maud and Miska Petersham, follows Bob, Betty, Paul, Peggy, and little Dot at school and on vacation. Bob wears a brown suit, Betty a checked dress, Paul a white blouse, Peggy curls, and Dot bobbed hair, all under teacher Miss West.

One morning Miss West hides a large round parcel on her desk, and the children guess balloon or football, both wrong. Through classroom surprises, games, and holidays, the book offers small readers a warm, orderly world where five friends learn, play, and look out for one another.
7846-departmental-ditties-and-ballads-an:
Rudyard Kipling's Departmental Ditties and Ballads and Barrack-Room Ballads joins two early volumes of verse on empire, office, and army life. The first runs from army headquarters and a legend of the Foreign Office through Uriah, public waste, and a code of morals to the last department.

The second brings the Ballad of East and West, the King's Mercy and Jest, Boh Da Thone, Danny Deever, Tommy, Fuzzy-Wuzzy, Gunga Din, Mandalay, and the Widow at Windsor. The opening lines eat bread and salt beside the dead, a pledge of shared life that runs through both books.
8393-life-in-the-backwoods:
Susanna Moodie wrote Life in the Backwoods as a sequel to Roughing It in the Bush, her famous account of settling in Upper Canada. Where the earlier book told of arrival and hardship, this volume sketches from nature. Its epigraph says the later life of a settler family is painful experience in a distant land, made her own, whether grave or gay.

Moodie, author of Life in the Clearings and Flora Lyndsay, writes with a settler's eye for neighbors, seasons, and the slow work of making a home. Readers of Canadian pioneer literature get a direct, often sharp voice, unsparing about both the bush and the people who came to it. The book stands as a classic of immigration writing.
8441-between-friends:
Robert W Chambers published Between Friends in 1914. It opens with Drene, a man who has entered into the obscurity of himself, like a man reentering a darkened house and lying down, aware of sunlight, bird-calls, and breeze outside. Through twilit corridors of his mind, Chambers follows a bruised soul, in the psychological manner of his later novels.

Chambers, once famous for weird tales, turned in his later years to society and psychological fiction, and this novel shows that turn. Readers get a story of friendship and inner life, told in the lush, slightly overwrought style Chambers favored. It suits readers tracing how popular novelists handled the new psychology of the 1910s.
8534-daily-strength-for-daily-needs:
Mary Wilder Tileston selected Daily Strength for Daily Needs, following her Joy and Strength for the Pilgrim's Day and Quiet Hours. Each day gives verses for strength, opening on January 1 with they go from strength to strength, and first the blade, then the ear. That the full corn in the ear, under the motto, as thy days, so shall thy strength be.

Tileston's devotional belongs to the Victorian habit of a verse for each morning, chosen to carry readers through the day. The selections draw on Scripture and hymns, arranged by calendar. Readers who keep a daily devotional will find a classic of the genre, plain, brief, and meant to be read slowly, one day at a time.
8777-authors-and-friends:
Annie Fields recalls the writers she knew in Authors and Friends. Opening with Chaucer's company of the leaf, whose laurel chaplets keep beauty fresh and green against every storm. Her contents read like a literary guest list: Longfellow from 1807 to 1882, glimpses of Emerson. Oliver Wendell Holmes with personal recollections and unpublished letters, days with Mrs Stowe, Celia Thaxter, Whittier's life and friendships, and Tennyson with Lady Tennyson.

Fields writes as a hostess and friend, not a critic, preserving talk, letters, and small kindnesses from Boston's golden age of letters. Longfellow's chapter begins with lilac buds bursting their sheaths each year, a fitting image for memory's return. Readers of American literature will find warm, firsthand portraits, best read as companions to the authors' own works rather than as formal biography.
9088-thoroughbreds:
W. A. Fraser wrote this novel of horse racing in upstate New York, dedicated to his wife, a thoroughbred herself. The scene is Brookfield, a village pinched into quiet isolation by a century of growth around it. Into its calm bursts horse racing, unearthed by Reverend Dolman and led by John Porter, called Honest John.

Porter's father raced in old Kentucky for sport, and the son kept the love. Fraser follows bets, breeds, and village talk with warmth. The novel charms as a tale of sport, character, and a small town stirred by speed and pride.
922-sunday-under-three-heads:
Charles Dickens wrote this short work on Sunday, dedicated to the Bishop of London. He takes Sunday under three heads, asking how the day should be kept, and for whom. His target is the strict Sabbatarian view that would shut the poor out of innocent recreation, while the rich enjoy their own Sundays in private.

Dickens argues with humour and humanity for a Sunday that allows rest, fresh air, and simple pleasures to working folk. The pamphlet shows his early social conscience and his gift for pleading a cause in plain prose. It remains a lively piece of Victorian debate, on a question that still divides opinion.
931-the-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert wrote these comic ballads under the pen name Bab, for the magazine Fun and later collections. Sailors, policemen, ghosts, and lovers tumble through topsy-turvy plots, told in brisk rhyme with a logic that turns sense on its head. The 1920 Macmillan edition gathers the set for a new generation.

Gilbert's humour is dry, precise, and absurd, and the ballads were the seed of his Savoy operas with Sullivan. Many types and jokes from the stage first appear here, in verse. The book is a treat for lovers of nonsense with a sharp edge, where rhyme and reason play a merry game.
933-more-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert gathered more of his Bab Ballads in this companion volume, with tales such as The Bumboat Woman's Story, The Two Ogres, Little Oliver, Mister William, and Pasha Bailey Ben. Lieutenant-Colonel Flare and other comic heroes follow, each caught in a plot where logic leads straight to folly.

Gilbert's verse is brisk and witty, with rhymes that snap and morals that wink. The ballads show the same topsy-turvy world as the first set, where rank, love, and law are turned upside down. The volume is a further feast for Gilbert fans, and a fine sample of Victorian comic verse at its most ingenious.
9405-the-book-of-old-english-ballads:
George Wharton Edwards gathered this book of old English ballads, with decorative drawings and an introduction by Hamilton Mabie, in 1896. Contents include Chevy Chace, King Cophetua and the Beggar-Maid, King Leir and his three daughters, and Fair Rosamond. Robin Hood tales, Barbara Allen, Sir Patrick Spens, and The Nut-brown Maid follow.

Mabie's introduction opens with Chevy Chace itself, a woeful hunting in the border hills. The ballads sing of love, war, and fate in old, plain speech. The book remains a handsome gateway to the ballad tradition, for readers and singers alike.
9482-what-sami-sings-with-the-birds:
Johanna Spyri, best known for Heidi, wrote What Sami Sings with the Birds, here in Helen B. Dole's 1917 translation. Sami is a poor Swiss boy whose hard life leaves him few joys, save the songs of birds by Lake Geneva. The tale follows him from Old Mary Ann's care to his grandmother's house, through want and loss. Birds, heard each spring, mark his hope.

As Sami grows, he learns to sing with the birds, and song steadies him through hard times. Spyri keeps the prose simple and the feeling warm, with Swiss fields, brooks, and ash trees close at hand. A reader gets a gentle story of a child who finds courage in nature and music, and a fine short companion to Spyri's better-known Alpine tales.
9500-farm-ballads:
Will Carleton wrote Farm Ballads, a book of poems drawn from farm life and country folk. Carleton says he wrote them in the open air, on trains, and in editors' rooms, then printed them in papers where readers met them with favor. Friends across the country asked him to gather them in lasting form. The book answers that call with plain, heartfelt verse.

Poems sing of teams afield, harvests, home, and the toil and humor of rural days. Carleton's voice is simple and direct, with a farmer's eye for work and weather. A reader gets a beloved set of American country poems, warm and easy to read aloud, from a poet who knew the fields first hand.
9649-with-trapper-jim-in-the-north-woods:
Lawrence J. Leslie wrote With Trapper Jim in the North Woods in 1913, a boys' camp tale of the Campfire and Trail series. Three chums reach Trapper Jim's hunting lodge in the far North Woods, led by luck and pluck. Toby Jucklin, the stuttering lad of broad shoulders, steals early scenes. Chapters promise woodcraft, trapping secrets, and a silver fox.

Later chapters track a thief, a clog trail, and a bruin surprise, with smoking out intruders and steady shooting beside. The boys learn the woods by doing, not by books. A reader gets a rousing outdoor adventure, full of camp lore, animal craft, and the fun of chums on the trail.
9778-vane-of-the-timberlands:
Harold Bindloss wrote Vane of the Timberlands, a novel of Canada's woods, coasts, and lumber camps. Vane, a young man of the timber country, faces a friend in need, a breeze down a fir-scented inlet, and an afternoon ashore. Chapters follow Vancouver, a sail north, a first mishap, and the bush, with floods, trails, and an intercepted letter. Lucy Vane, Jessy, and Evelyn cross his path.

Later chapters bring a search, a flood, and convincing testimony, till Vane is reinstated at the last. Bindloss writes with brisk, outdoor verve. A reader gets a rousing Canadian adventure, full of canoes, camps, and a hero's fight for his name.
9852-the-man-from-the-clouds:
J. Storer Clouston's 1919 novel opens with a man found on a shore after coming down from the clouds. A small community takes him in, but a suspicious stranger, a doctor, and questions about who he is soon unsettle the place.

As the story moves into its second part, an idea, a little dinner, and a test bring the stranger's secret closer to exposure, with a pursuer named Bolton on the track. Clouston keeps the mystery light and brisk. Readers get a puzzle about identity, told with humor and a seaside setting.
9854-frank-roscoe-s-secret-or-the-darewe:
Allen Chapman's 1908 boys' book follows Frank Roscoe and his Darewell chums on a woodland holiday that turns into a mystery. The boys plan a dinner, stumble on a conspiracy, and watch as Ned is captured and hears strange talk in the woods.

Suspicions grow around a stranger in town and a neighbor's queer behavior, while the chums camp, race, and use a telephone wire to untangle the plot. Chapman writes in the brisk school-story manner of his day. Young readers get friendship, camping fun, and a secret worth guarding.
a-book-of-golden-deeds:
A Book of Golden Deeds, published in 1864 by Charlotte M Yonge, gathers true tales of brave and selfless acts. Yonge was a popular Victorian novelist and writer for young readers. Rather than inventing a story, she collected real deeds of heroism from history and retold them in short, clear accounts meant to be remembered.

Each tale shows someone choosing courage, loyalty, or sacrifice at a hard moment, often at risk to their own life. Together the stories form a kind of moral gallery, offered to readers as examples worth copying. The book was a Victorian favorite for family and school reading, and it shows how the age taught character through story.
a-bundle-of-ballads:
Henry Morley edited this gathering of old English ballads, with an introduction on the minstrels who once carried such songs from house to house. The contents open with Chevy Chase in two versions, then The Nut-Brown Maid and the outlaw tale of Adam Bell, Clym of the Clough, and William of Cloudeslie. A glossary closes the book.

Robin Hood rides here, with Sir Patrick Spens, Edward Edward, Barbara Allen's Cruelty, The Children in the Wood, and Casabianca. Morley, a tireless editor of cheap classics for working readers, chose ballads for story and singability alike. The volume is a pocket library of the people's poetry, from border raids to ghostly lovers.
a-collection-of-ballads:
Andrew Lang edited this gathering of old English and Scottish ballads, first published in 1897 and reprinted in 1910, with an introduction and notes. The contents open with Sir Patrick Spens, the Battle of Otterbourne, Tam Lin, and Thomas the Rhymer. Many of the songs are centuries old and were carried by singing rather than by print.

The ballads tell of sea wrecks, border raids, fairies, ghosts, true love, murder, and betrayal, in short stanzas made to be sung. Names like Kinmont Willie, Johnnie Armstrong, and the Twa Sisters fill the list. Lang chose well-loved versions, so the book works as a first shelf of the folk ballad tradition.
allan-and-the-ice-gods:
Allan and the Ice Gods, published in 1927 by H Rider Haggard, is the final volume of the Allan Quatermain saga. It forms the fourth part of a loosely linked series that began with Allan and the Holy Flower. Quatermain, Haggard's famous hunter hero, once more takes the hallucinogenic taduki drug, as he did in earlier novels of the series.

Under the drug, he finds himself reliving a past life as Wi, a civilized man living in the barbaric ice age as part of a clan of cavemen. The device lets Haggard set a modern mind inside a prehistoric struggle for survival. The book closes the Quatermain sequence with its strangest journey, into deep time rather than across Africa.
an-unprotected-female-at-the-pyramids:
Anthony Trollope tells a tale of Egypt from the 1864 Chapman and Hall collection Tales of All Countries. He begins by remembering how Grand Cairo filled his young imagination from the Arabian Nights: fantastic houses, beautiful or cunning women, and good-natured, capricious monarchs. The grown traveler finds a different Egypt, full of tourists.

Among them is an English lady traveling without protector or chaperone, determined to see the Pyramids on her own terms. Guides, dragomans, fellow tourists, and a persistent admirer test her independence at every step. Trollope, who knew the tourist world well, mixes satire of travelers' pretensions with real sympathy for his heroine's nerve.
ballads:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Ballads, in its second edition of 1895, gathers his long narrative poems drawn from Pacific and Scottish legend. The Song of Rahero tells a Tahitian tale of slaying and vengeance, with Stevenson's own notes attached. The Feast of Famine does the same for Marquesan manners.

Ticonderoga retells a West Highland legend about a name that brings doom, and Heather Ale recalls the last makers of the Picts' secret drink. Stevenson wrote these poems during his South Seas years, testing whether ballad meter could carry foreign folklore without flattening it. The notes show how carefully he learned the stories from island tellers and Highland tradition.
barrack-room-ballads:
Rudyard Kipling's barrack-room verse fills two series here, the first of 1892 and the second of 1896, forty songs and ballads in all. The dedication is to Thomas Atkins, the ordinary British soldier, in the person of T. A. The contents list the famous names: Danny Deever, Tommy, Fuzzy-Wuzzy, Gunga Din, and Mandalay.

Kipling writes in the soldier's own barrack slang, cockney dropped aitches and all. The subjects are the private's whole world: hangings and route marches, cholera camps and loot, the Widow at Windsor, and the long sail home in Troopin'. Gentlemen-Rankers gives the ruined officer serving in the ranks his own bitter song. No book of verse did more to put the common soldier's voice into English poetry.
beasts-men-and-gods:
Ferdinand Ossendowski's Beasts, Men and Gods carries an explanatory note vouching for its author, a Polish scientist, whom Dr Albert Shaw called the Robinson Crusoe of the twentieth century. The editor admits the adventures seem too highly colored to be real. Part one, Drawing Lots with Death, follows Ossendowski's flight from Bolshevik Siberia in 1920, through forests, frozen rivers, and Red partisans.

Part two enters Mongolia, where he meets the Baron Ungern, the mad White general who took Urga, and hears prophecies in mysterious Tibet. A young woman's corruption shows him, he writes, what depravity Bolshevism brought into the world. The book was a 1922 sensation; historians still argue over how much Ossendowski embroidered.
berlin-and-sans-souci-or-frederick-the-g:
L. Mühlbach's Berlin and Sans-Souci continues her Frederick the Great romances, following the king from the throne room to his beloved palace of carefree ease. Sans-Souci, the little vineyard palace at Potsdam, gives the book its second capital: there Frederick plays the flute, writes French verse, and gathers philosophers instead of courtiers. Voltaire's residence at court stands at the story's center, friendship curdling into rivalry. Berlin supplies the counterweight of guards, parade, and the king's Spartan discipline.

Mühlbach, whose header here reads Louise Muhlbach, writes the enlightened court as domestic drama. Ministers, generals, mistresses of ceremony, and the king's family circle through receptions, concerts, and campaigns' returns. Readers who finished Frederick the Great and His Court get the reign's second act here, the philosopher-king whose friendships were waged like his wars.
bleek-mantis-friends:
Dorothea Bleek edited The Mantis and His Friends for print in 1924. The tales come from her father Wilhelm Bleek's old notebooks. /Xam storytellers had dictated them in the 1870s at Cape Town.

The trickster Mantis leads a cast of beasts, stars, and spirits. His pranks, lusts, and sorrows shape a whole mythic world here. The tales rank as the richest first record of San oral art. Bleek's team caught the voice of tellers whose world was vanishing. Readers meet Bushman folklore at its source, strange and deeply human throughout. The Mantis himself shifts from fool to maker within a single tale.
cap-n-warren-s-wards:
Joseph C Lincoln's novel Cap'n Warren's Wards appeared in 1911, published in New York by D Appleton and Company. New York lawyer Atwood Graves rides a storm-delayed train to Cape Cod on unwelcome business. His errand concerns Captain Elisha Warren, a retired sea captain living quietly in South Denboro. Warren's dead brother has named him guardian of two children.

Caroline Warren is nearly twenty, and her brother Stephen is a year younger. Neither has ever met their uncle, and both resent the arrangement. Graves explains the will, its trust money, and Warren's right to refuse. The captain must decide where the young people will live and how strictly to rule them. Lincoln builds a warm village comedy about family duty, young pride, and an old sailor learning parenthood late.
catalogue-of-british-columbia-birds:
Catalogue of British Columbia Birds, by Francis Kermode, curator of the Provincial Museum at Victoria, lists every bird proven to occur in the province. Kermode dates his preface August 1904. He aims at completeness and admits failure in advance. The list is incomplete, he says, especially for the northern interior. That country, he is sure, is a valuable field for work. The late John Fannin's 1898 list held three hundred thirty nine species and subspecies. Kermode adds twenty four.

Observers across the province supplied local lists, notes, and specimens. Brooks in the Okanagan, Keen in the Queen Charlotte Islands, and Green at Fairview are thanked by name. The catalogue then proceeds by order and family, from the diving birds and grebes onward. Each entry fixes a species to British Columbia on evidence. Museum science here is a network of country observers, mailing skins and sightings to Victoria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-african-synod:
African Synods were not general councils of the entire church, since none was ever held in North Africa. They were many national or plenary bishop assemblies for the North African church, commonly called African or Carthaginian Synods. They must not be confused with district or provincial assemblies, also very numerous in the separate provinces. Those Roman provinces lay between Sahara and Mediterranean, from Cyrenaica east to the Atlantic west, roughly modern Tripoli, Algeria, and Morocco.

There the church entered history late in the second century and vanished early in the eighth. About the mid-third century, bishops of the three civil provinces formed a single ecclesiastical province. As dioceses multiplied, they grouped into divisions matching political divisions. Diocletian redistricted North Africa into six civil provinces; by the late fourth century the church had adjusted to those lines, yielding six ecclesiastical provinces lasting until the Arab invasion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-breads:
Altar breads are one of the two elements required for the Eucharist. Whether Christ used ordinary table bread cannot be told from the sacred text. In the Western Church the breads were probably round, as catacomb pictures show, and Pope St. Zephyrinus called the altar bread a round crown-like offering. Eastern churches use round or square breads.

For valid consecration the host must use wheaten flour and pure natural water, oven-baked or pressed between heated irons, and uncorrupted. Western bread is unleavened, Eastern bread leavened, except among Maronites and Armenians. The large host usually bears Christ crucified, and the breads took many names as sacrament or sacrifice, including gift and host.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-cards:
Altar cards print the prayers a celebrant should know by heart, standing at the altar's middle and each end. They date only from the sixteenth century, and bishops do not use them, reading all prayers from the Pontifical Canon. At Pius V's Missal revision only the middle card existed, called the Tabella Secretarum. Later the Gospel of St. John joined it on the Gospel side, and the Deus qui humanae substantiae prayer with the Lavabo psalm on the Epistle side for symmetry.

Only during Mass do the cards rest on the altar, the middle one against crucifix or tabernacle, the side ones against candlesticks or altar steps. At other times they are removed or laid face down under the altar cover, and when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed outside Mass they must be removed. Framed cards should match the altar's architecture as far as possible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beguines-begh:
Beguines and Beghards take names most likely from old Flemish beghen, to pray, not to beg, since neither community was mendicant. Other guesses invoke St Bega of Nivelles or Lambert le Bègue, founder of a Liège cloister for crusaders' widows. From the early twelfth century, women in the Netherlands lived alone, vowless, devoted to prayer and good works. Their numbers swelled in the Crusades' age of desolate women, and about 1200 some grouped their cabins into the first Beguinage.

A Beguine was hardly a nun: she took no vows, could wed and return to the world, and kept her property. If poor, she lived by manual labor or teaching burghers' children, not by alms. They waned with the cloth trade, battered by the Reformation's storm and broken by the French Revolution. Belgian foundations fell from ninety-four to twenty by 1856, with membership about 1,600 that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-o: The Brothers of Our Lady of the Fields, a Canadian congregation founded in 1902 at Saint-Damien de Buckland in the Quebec diocese by Father M. J.-O. Brousseau, train orphans in farm and trade work and in settlement arts. The Sisters of Notre Dame of Perpetual Help, founded likewise by Brousseau in 1892, care for the orphans until age twelve, when the brothers take them over. The mother-house stands at Saint-Damien, Bellechasse County, Lac Vert, and the community now counts six brothers and four novices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camisards:
The Camisards, likely named for their black work blouse, the camise, worn as a uniform, were French fanatics who terrorized Dauphiné, Vivarais, and above all the Cévennes early in the eighteenth century. Their roots lay in the lingering Albigensian spirit, the apocalyptic preaching of French Calvinists, and Louis XIV's harsh methods of conversion after the Edict of Nantes was revoked in 1685. The murder of the Abbé de Chaila in 1702 opened open war.

Armed bands under Séguier, Laporte, Castanet, Ravenel, and Cavalier fought a guerrilla war until about 1705, when they surrendered or were destroyed, and Cavalier's 1709 attempt to revive the revolt failed. A peace treaty with England in 1711 cut off their support, and on 8 March 1715 Louis XIV proclaimed the sect wholly extinct. Much debate surrounds their prophets, some writers holding that Du Serre trained young recruits in a school of prophecy, while Calvinist writers deny any such school existed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caroline-isla:
East of the Philippines in the Pacific lie the Caroline Islands, some 500 small coral islands. Yap, one of the larger islands, lies 1,200 miles from Manila. Spaniards discovered the group in the sixteenth century and named it for Charles V. Jesuit missionaries John Anthony Cantova and Victor Walter tried the mission in 1731, but Cantova was soon murdered and Walter forced to flee, with two more Jesuits killed later.

After the Jesuits' suppression in 1767, no missionary trace appears for 120 years, until Leo XIII settled a German-Spanish dispute for Spain and Spanish Capuchins arrived in March 1886. The Propaganda set up the mission that May in West and East sections, formerly under the Vicariate of Micronesia. The islanders, of Polynesian race, lived by hunting and fishing without farming. A Jesuit weather station on Yap, begun in 1905, cabled typhoon warnings to Manila twice daily.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-und:
Patrick Toner's long entry treats Communion under both kinds, set against Communion under one kind alone. One kind means bread alone or wine alone. Both kinds mean distinct reception under bread and wine together, sub utraque specie. Toner works under three heads: Catholic doctrine and modern discipline, history of disciplinary change, and theological speculation. The priest's Communion under both kinds belongs at least to the sacrifice's integrity, and for some theologians to its essence.

History runs from the first century to the twelfth, when public Communion in East and West ordinarily ran under both kinds. Variations fill the record: sick Communion under bread alone at Alexandria, children's Communion before reason, the Presanctified Mass, and intinction, forbidden at Braga. The Utraquist controversy tested the doctrine, and John chapter six supplied texts for both sides. Speculation closes by weighing whether the chalice adds grace by prolonging the species and fervor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faroe-islands:
The Faroe Islands are a Danish group some four hundred miles west of Norway. Fourteen inhabited islands span about 500 square miles of dark, rocky ground. Sheep graze the flowery pastures, and over 100,000 live outdoors all year-round. Fishing, cattle, and bird-catching feed the 16,000 islanders.

Irish monks found the islands first, and Norsemen settled them soon after. Norway ruled them until 1814, and twenty-three Catholic bishops served there. The Reformation ended Catholic life by the close of the sixteenth century. An unfinished Gothic cathedral at Kirkebö still recalls the Catholic age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-islan:
The Gilbert Islands form a vicariate apostolic of sixteen low atolls near the Equator, the easternmost link of Micronesia, together with the Ellice and Panapa islands. Its chief atolls include Tapiteuca, Arorai, Apemama, Maiana, Marakei, and Nonouti. A Catholic Encyclopedia article describes a people under nominal British protection but practically self-governing, living chiefly by copra.

The vicariate was erected on 17 July 1897, when the Vicariate of Micronesia was divided, under Mgr. Joseph Leray of the Congregation of the Sacred Heart. Of a population reckoned at thirty to forty thousand, fourteen thousand were Catholics. Twelve churches and fifty-six chapels served them, with nineteen priests and ninety-six parish schools. Twelve orphanages sheltered four hundred children, beside houses of religious men and women.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grand-rapids:
Grand Rapids is a diocese created on 12 May 1882 from Detroit, covering the lower peninsula of Michigan north of Ottawa, Montcalm, Gratiot, and Saginaw, an area of 22,561 square miles. At its creation it held about fifty thousand Catholics served by thirty-four priests. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diocese that prospered steadily under its first bishop.

Henry Joseph Richter, born at Neuenkirchen in Oldenburg in 1838, was ordained at Rome in 1865. He was consecrated at Grand Rapids in April 1883. Belgian and Dutch colonies, with Irish admixture and later Poles, settled its rural regions. By the article's statistics the diocese counted 133 priests, 91 churches with resident priests, 66 parish schools with 13,545 pupils, and a Catholic population of 126,057.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guilds:
Medieval guilds were voluntary associations for worship, fellowship, and trade, reaching their height among the Teutonic peoples, above all the English. The entry sorts them into four kinds, religious guilds, peace or frith guilds, merchant guilds, and craft guilds, and traces the word itself to an Anglo-Saxon verb meaning to pay.

English evidence runs from Ina's seventh-century laws and the Abbotsbury charter under Canute, with its almsgiving, sick care, burials. Masses, to merchant guilds that guarded town trade monopolies, fined outsiders, watched the quality of goods, and doubled as the town's governing body. Craft guilds, later chapters, and the guilds' slow decline carry a vast survey that opens with Brentano's theory of family origins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-imposition-of:
Laying hands on someone is a symbolic rite meant to pass on a gift, a quality, or an excellence, most often spiritual, or to appoint a person to an office. People have used it for worldly ends as well as sacred ones. It reaches back to patriarchal days.

Jacob gave Ephraim and Manasses blessing and inheritance by laying hands on them, and Moses handed Hebrew leadership to Josue the same way. In the New Testament, the Lord used the rite to bring Jairus's daughter back to life and to heal the sick. Its sacred use shows first when Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests, and when priests placed hands on animals offered in sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ionian-island:
Seven islands west of Greece, with their islets, make up the Heptanesus of this geography entry. Corfu, Paxos, Leucadia or Santa Maura, Ithaca, Cephalonia, Zante, and Cerigo stretch between 36 and 40 degrees north. Together they cover about 1,095 square miles. Their population is put at 261,930. Most islanders belonged to the Greek Orthodox Church, with 6,615 Latin-rite Catholics, a few thousand Jews, and a small Muslim minority.

Mild and healthy air and mountain land still yielded cotton, wine, oil, and raisins in fair amount. The entry's real weight lies in the islands' tangled past and in Catholic life among an Orthodox majority, from bishops and churches to the Latin minority's standing. Readers get both a map and a short history of a borderland between East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-shields:
Soldier and senator James Shields, born at Dungannon, County Tyrone, Ireland, on 12 December 1810, died at Ottumwa, Iowa, on 1 June 1879. After emigrating to America in 1826 he took up law at once, opening practice at Kaskaskia, Illinois, in 1832. Illinois voters sent him to the state legislature in 1836, and he went on to serve as state auditor in 1839 and judge of the state supreme court in 1843. War with Mexico found him commissioner of the general land office.

Commissioned brigadier general by President Polk on 1 July 1846, Shields served with distinction under Taylor, Wool, and Scott. He won a major-general's brevet at Cerro Gordo, where a shot passed through his lung. Severely wounded again at Chapultepec, he mustered out in 1848, then governed Oregon Territory briefly before resigning to sit in the United States Senate for Illinois as a Democrat. His life runs from battlefield to Senate chamber.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-edmund:
Julian Edmund Tenison Woods was an English-born Australian priest, scientist, and founder. Born at Southwark in London in 1832, he worked for the Times, tried the Passionists, and taught at Toulon, where he caught a love of geology. In 1854 he sailed with Bishop Willson to Tasmania as a schools assistant and was ordained at Adelaide in 1857.

Given a parish of twenty-two thousand square miles around Penola, Woods founded the Sisters of St. Joseph of the Sacred Heart in 1866 with Mary MacKillop, and the Brothers of the Sacred Heart in 1869. He also preached missions across three colonies for eleven years. He died at Sydney in 1889, honored as priest and naturalist alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lauds:
Lauds, meaning praises, is the Roman office of psalms and canticles usually said after Matins, whose whole purpose is praising God. Its name comes from the office's last three psalms, 148, 149, and 150, where laudate rings out again and again.

At first Lauds named only those three psalms with their conclusion, as Greek Ainoi and St. Benedict's Rule still show, while the whole dawn office passed as Matutinum in the fifth and sixth centuries. Gradually Lauds swallowed the whole office and Matins became the Night Office instead. The word also meant the Mass alleluia after the Epistle, in Toledo's phrase, and the public acclamations shouted at a prince's accession, long kept in church on set occasions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leeds:
Leeds is a diocese covering Yorkshire's West Riding and York south of the Ouse. It is one of fourteen in the Westminster province, though it was not erected at Pius IX's 1850 restoration of the English hierarchy. That year Rome created Beverley for all Yorkshire, anticipating its later division, from the Yorkshire District formed in 1840 out of the Northern District of 1688.

John Briggs, St. Cuthbert's College president and last vicar apostolic of a vast northern territory, became Beverley's first bishop, counting about 180,000 Catholics in 1839, only 13,000 in Yorkshire. His episcopate was a heroic struggle for schools and churches for a destitute, Irish-immigrant population, with thousands of Yorkshire children receiving no Catholic schooling at all. Robert Cornthwaite succeeded him in 1861 and won the 1878 brief dividing Beverley, though it stayed unpublished until February 1879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-literary-or-p:
Literary or profane legends are the great hero tales that grew up where early history shades into story, told and retold until they took fixed literary shape. This long survey treats them as a group, asking how spoken tales gain detail, lose facts, borrow motifs, and harden into books.

Germanic hero saga opens the run, followed by Charlemagne and Roland, Genevieve of Brabant, and Arthur. Then come Tristan and Isolde, Lohengrin, Tannhauser, Robert the Devil, the Wandering Jew, the Flying Dutchman, William Tell, and Faust. Each section retells the tale, weighs its sources, and sorts what may be history from what is pure fancy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-us:
Creeds in worship began with baptism, where converts learned and recited the faith before receiving the sacrament. That use appears as early as Hippolytus and Cyril of Jerusalem, and may be older still, so wide was its spread.

At the Eucharist the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed entered at Antioch in 471 and Constantinople in 511, though Rome held back until the eleventh century. The entry then maps creed use rite by rite: Roman, Ambrosian, Gallican, Mozarabic, Celtic, and Anglican, plus the Eastern churches. Each rite has its own place for the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene Creed, or a local form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lollards:
Lollards were the followers of John Wyclif, a dissenting body thick in England from the late fourteenth century into the first half of the fifteenth. The nickname reached them in 1382, when Henry Crumpe used it at Oxford, and bishops' papers took it up by 1387.

England had long been free of heresy, yet anger at clerical wealth, pride, and power ran deep. War in France, plague, and social strain fed the mood, and Wyclif's teaching gave it a voice. The entry traces the causes of the spread, the doctrines condemned by church courts, and the sect's fate under persecution, from pulpit preaching to revolt and suppression.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mariana-islan:
Mariana Islands, also called the Ladrones, form a chain of fifteen islands in the northern Pacific, between 13 and 21 degrees north and 144 and 146 degrees east. Magellan found them in 1521 and named them Thieves' Islands for native thieving. Spain planted a regular colony in 1667 and renamed them Marianas for Queen Maria Anna of Austria.

Their people then numbered 40,000 to 60,000, but fierce resistance nearly wiped them out before Spanish rule held. Spain kept them under the Philippines until 1898, when Guam passed to the United States after the Spanish-American War. In 1899 the rest, with the Carolines, were sold to Germany for about four million dollars. Guam, 32 miles long and about 200 square miles, held 11,490 people, with Agana capital at 7,000, serving as a United States naval station. A prefecture apostolic of 1902, entrusted to Westphalian Capuchins in 1907, served a wholly Catholic people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquesas-isl:
Marquesas Islands, in Polynesia, numbered eleven islands between 7 and 10 degrees south and 138 and 141 degrees west, covering 480 square miles. Their people, called cannibals in the entry, lived mainly by fishing in huts of wattles and branches. Breadfruit, coconut, banana, orange, and sugar cane were chief crops, with horses, pigs, sheep, cotton, and tobacco brought by missionaries.

Mendana found them in 1595 and named them for the Marquess de Mendoza, then Viceroy of Peru, and the first Mass was said there on 28 July 1595. Picpus missionaries landed at Vaithu on 4 August 1836 and found natives given to tattooing and cruel, defective morals. Whalers had left phthisis in 1774, and population fell from 17,700 in 1804 to 8,000 in 1830 and about half that later. Baptisms rose from 216 adults in 1838 to 1848 to 986 in 1848 to 1856. Schools at Taiohae taught 300 children in 1900, and by 1900 opium and alcohol were banned and schooling compulsory, though France's Associations Law closed the schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marshall-isla:
Marshall Islands were a German Pacific possession since 1885, east of the Carolines, between 4 and 13 degrees north and 161 and 171 degrees east. Spanish sailors found them in 1529, and Marshall and Gilbert explored them in 1788. Fifty low atolls, highest point just thirty-three feet, with Nauru included, covered about 150 square miles.

Population in 1908 reached 15,000, only 162 Europeans, most natives still pagan. Sacred Heart missionaries began in 1891, were forced out by civil authorities, and resumed in 1898. The islands first joined the New Pomerania vicariate, then became a separate vicariate in September 1905, without episcopal character yet. Superior Augustus Erdland lived on Jaluit. By 1907 the mission counted seven priests, eight brothers, thirteen sisters, 323 Catholics, 520 catechumens, six churches and stations, and eight schools with 225 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-national-syno:
National synods, by recent canon law, are deliberating assemblies where all bishops of a nation meet, convoked by patriarch or primate. To cover ancient synods too, it is better to call them a legitimate assemblage of a nation's episcopate, whose decisions bind an entire national Church. The classic definition fits ancient councils poorly, just as it fits ecumenical councils imperfectly.

Councils divide into general or ecumenical and particular, with particular ones split into national and provincial by their scope. Diocesan clergy assemblies are diocesan synods rather than councils. Writers warn the classification cannot be exact. Arles in 314, where Constantine with the pope gathered the empire's episcopate, and African bishops' assemblies, test the boundaries. The entry sorts the kinds, their authority, and their place in church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippine-is:
The Philippine Islands were an archipelago of 3,141 islands between the China Sea and the Pacific, south of Japan and north of Borneo. Luzon covers 40,969 square miles and Mindanao 36,292, with a total land area of 115,026. Mount Apo in Mindanao tops 10,000 feet, Mayon rises as the world's most symmetrical volcanic cone, and the Cagayan, Rio Grande, and Agusan run over 200 miles. This vast Catholic Encyclopedia survey treats land, peoples, history, and church.

Magellan reached the islands, and Legaspi sailed from Mexico in 1564 with the Augustinian Urdaneta, founding Spanish rule that friars then civilized for centuries. Later sections count peoples and faiths, trace the American occupation, and reckon a Catholic population above five million served by secular clergy and fewer than 500 religious in 1906. Missions among Moros, schools, and dioceses complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seleucids:
The Seleucids were the Macedonian dynasty founded by Seleucus, a general of Alexander the Great, which ruled Syria from 312 BC. This entry opens with Seleucus receiving Babylonia in 321, losing it to Antigonus, and winning it back after Gaza in 312. That year starts the era counted from his name. Taking the royal title in 306, he subdued upper Asia to the Indus and gained Syria at Ipsus. He founded the great residential cities of Seleucia on the Tigris and Antioch on the Orontes.

His son Antiochus I Soter moved the court to Antioch for fear of the Parthians. Under Antiochus II Theos the long wars with Egypt over Phoenicia and Palestine began. A marriage alliance with Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, paused the fighting. After Ptolemy's death the disowned first wife Laodice returned and took revenge. The entry carries the dynasty's tangled succession forward from there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-southern-solo:
The Southern Solomon Islands prefecture took its name from a Spanish explorer's hopeful guess, and this entry traces the islands from first European contact to mission days. Alvaro Mendana de Neyra found Ysabel, Guadalcanar, and San Christoval in 1567, named the group for King Solomon after admiring its natural riches. And saw Mass said by his Franciscan chaplain before sailing back to Peru.

A second voyage in 1595, carrying 368 emigrants, landed at Santa Cruz and ended with Mendana's death two months later, his widow and pilot bringing the survivors home to Spain. The entry then turns to the modern prefecture, its parishes and missionaries, giving readers both the romance of discovery and the slow work of building a church in the Pacific.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bahama-is:
A chain of coral islands north of Cuba and east of southern Florida is surveyed here, the most northerly group of the West Indies. Twenty-five islands hold permanent settlements, with countless cays and rocks besides, stretched between about 21 and 27 degrees north. Nassau, on New Providence, the only island with a safe harbour, serves as capital.

Origins of the names Bahama and Lucayos, the latter from Spanish Los Cayos, open the account. Population, largely of African descent through slavery, follows, with emancipation on 1 August 1834, when 10,086 slaves were freed and owners paid compensation. Church history, schools, and missions round out a portrait of island life at the start of the twentieth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-canary-is:
Seven chief islands and scattered islets off Africa's western coast form the archipelago described here, lying between about 27 and 29 degrees north. Lanzarote and Fuerteventura stand nearest the mainland, then Tenerife and Gran Canaria, with Palma, Gomera, and Hierro farther west. Their total area runs about 3,256 square miles, and the 1900 census counted 358,564 people.

Mountainous and volcanic throughout, the islands crown themselves in Tenerife's Pico de Teyde at 12,200 feet. Caverns, springs, and torrents mark the landscape, while dromedaries and canary-birds enliven a fauna otherwise European. Conquest, church foundations, and missions complete a compact island history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-five-sacr:
Hands, feet, and side of Christ, pierced in the Passion, anchor the devotion described here. Religious revival under Bernard and Francis in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, joined to crusaders returning from the Holy Land, gave fresh force to honouring the Five Wounds. A Mass and an Office grew around them.

Polish bishops told Clement XIII why these parts deserved special cult: they bore special pains for salvation and shine as marks of love. Beads, images, confraternities, and feasts spread the practice, which the entry follows through prayer books and popular piety. Readers see how a meditation on suffering became a lasting form of prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-netherlan:
Low Countries under Charles V and his heirs form the historical sweep here, from Burgundian lands to Spanish and then Austrian Netherlands. Charles's organisation joined what is now Holland and Belgium, and later histories of Burgundy and Charles himself carry the earlier tale. Holland's secession as the United Provinces in 1579 sheared the north away.

Philip II, succeeding his father, found the seventeen provinces at their zenith of wealth and good government, as Guicciardini wrote in 1567. Antwerp had replaced Bruges as the trading queen. Religious revolt, war with Spain, and the slow forging of two nations follow, with church life, art, and commerce woven through a long and tangled history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-washing-of-fe:
Washing of feet and hands treats a courtesy owed to guests in sandal-wearing Eastern lands from earliest times, given deep religious meaning by Christ's action after the Last Supper in John 13. Down to St Bernard, church writers sometimes called the ceremony a sacrament in the wider sense, meaning it held the virtue of what we now call a sacramental.

Christ's command to wash one another's feet was understood literally from the start, Paul implying that a widow honoured by the Church should be one who had washed the saints' feet. Tradition, the entry argues, never broke, though early evidence is scattered. Elvira's council in AD 300 directed that baptismal candidates' feet be washed not by priests but by clerics or layfolk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-reyno:
William Reynolds, also Rainolds, was an English Catholic scholar who helped translate the Reims Testament. Born near Exeter about 1544, second son of Richard Rainolds and elder brother of John Rainolds, an Authorized Version scholar, he died at Antwerp in 1594. Schooled at Winchester, he became a fellow of New College, Oxford, from 1560 to 1572. The Jewel-Harding controversy and Allen's personal sway converted him, and in 1575 he publicly recanted at Rome.

Reynolds studied for the priesthood at Douai from 1577, moved with the college to Reims in 1578, and took orders at Châlons in April 1580. He stayed to lecture on Scripture and Hebrew and to aid Gregory Martin's Reims Testament translation. Later he served as chaplain to the Beguines at Antwerp. His books include a refutation of Whitaker's attack on Reims, a 1590 treatise on Christian commonwealths against impious kings under the name Rossaeus, a sacrament treatise, and Calvino-Turcismus.
city-ballads: City Ballads, Will Carleton's urban poems. The city's verse. This book preserves that poetry. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
cross-roads:
Margaret E. Sangster gathered her magazine poems in Cross Roads, a book named for the choice-points where her preface sonnet leaves the reader standing. Sangster writes of woods and city windows, tenement mothers and Fifth Avenue, gloves, porcelain puppies, and old schoolhouses, all in plain rhymes meant to be understood at first hearing. Many pieces first ran in the Christian Herald and Good Housekeeping.

The last part turns to war: poems on Château-Thierry, ruined churches, transports, and a prayer for boys killed in action, closing with Independence Day 1919. Sangster, an editor as well as a poet, aimed at consolation rather than experiment. The collection maps what ordinary American magazine readers asked poetry to do between the wars of her lifetime.
dick-hamilton-s-airship-or-a-young-milli:
Howard R Garis wrote Dick Hamilton's Airship, or A Young Millionaire in the Clouds, for his boys' series about the richest lad in America. The contents open with a falling biplane and a colonel's offer: a twenty-thousand-dollar prize for a transcontinental flight. Dick resolves to build an airship with a stabilizer of his own design and enter.

Army aviators, suspicions of spies, and Dick's first flight lead to Hamilton Corners, where his miserly Uncle Ezra visits, acts queerly, and even flies, with an accident to follow. The government will assign an officer to the flight and may buy the winning patent. Garis, creator of Uncle Wiggily, keeps the machinery simple and the pace brisk.
